For years, whenever my Customers hive asked me for a Mild Tes, I have advised the Pare. old Fisk:limed China which I keep, and the advice has been appreciated. It is very satisfactory to them that such an eminent authority as Sir Andrew Clarke, the London Physician, corroborates opinion. Here is an extract from an interesting lecture, delivered by Sir Andrew the other day. to •the Students of the Undon Hospital : "Tea is a blessed beverage. Ido not know what I should do without it. But there is tea and tea, an.l one of the teas I have in my mind is the representation of all that is physiologically wleked. Igo about town a good deal holding consulta- tions hero and there, and about five o'clock, when I get into a place. the lady of the housG will say to me : • Sir Andrew, you look tired, do let me give you a cup of tea.' I say • thank you very much. But the tea has stood for half-an-hour, and she remarks, 'I know you do you not like it strong, Sir Andrew, and she then pours about a tablespoonful of the tea into a cup and fills thecup up with water. Now I call it positivecruelty to give tea like that to anybody and I hope you, gentlemen, will always set your face against it. Tea, to be useful, should be first of all Black China Tea ; the Indian Tea which is being cultivated has become so powertul in its effects upon the nervms system that a cup of it taken early in the morning, as many do. so disorders the nervous system that those who take it actually get into a state of tea intoxication, and It produces a form of nervous disturbance, which is most painful to witness. It you want to have, either for yourselves or for your patients, tea which will not injure and which will refresh, get Black China Tea, putting in the right measure—the old fashioned teaspoonful for each person and one for the blessed pot. Then pour on briskly boiling water, and within five minutes you must pour It off again, or it will become wicked instead of good." Such is Sir Andrew Clarke's opinion: and advise. A few words of warning, however, are necessary to those who have for gotten what this old fashioned ea is Bk.:. " WHY, It is as plain as that two and two make tour." "But I deny that too; for two and two , make twenty-two." ,A,CITIZEN of Cork being asked one morning how he "came by that black eye," answered that he - "slept on his fist." IT may seem paradoxical, but it is nevertheless true, that a man cannot smoke a cigar too short unless he smokes it too long. "Groans WASHINGTON NArOLEON JACEIBON HANNIBAL HARRISON." "Yes, rna'arn•" "Ten Josephine Regina Cleopatra Matilda Victoria to bring up the slop-pail." "Yes, ma'am." "BATHING Suers" is a sign that frequent;y stares one in the face now-a-days, and there is no doubt that bathing suits alavast everybody this ;hot weather. A CRITIC, in noticing a discourse on "The Say- ings and Doings of Great Men," remarks.: " It is sad to observe how much they said and how 'little they did." A cotrxrax doctor being asked what was the best way to cure a hatn, remarked that before answering that question he should want to know what ailed the ham. AN old farmer, the first time he ate an oyster stew, was asked how he liked it: Well,' he answered, " I liked the soup well enough, but I wish they'd leftout them pollywogs:" No, my dear, I would mot wear tan- coloured gloves—they don't match your -dress." His heiress: " Dear me—neither ido they But then"—brightening—"you know, papa, I can get a dress and a wrap and a bonnet and a parasol to match the gloves." A N.c NICEx of ladies on a -steamboat on the Thames were h•arrified on having an ordinary. looking man ameng the passengers pointed out to them as one "who had buried seventeen wives." He was a grave-digger, hut that didn't occur to the horrified ladies. Tow —" You have over rret my wife, John. Permit me." Jehn to the bride " Ah, pleased, I ass-izre you. Know you well, though— very well." The bride—"'Sir I" John—" Tom has shown me lots of lettcra from his dear Lizzie." The bride—" Sir I My nànb is Amelia." As Jerrold was walking to the club with a friend from the theatre, some intoxicated young gentle- men reeled up to the dramatist and said, "Can you tell us the way to the Judge and Jury ?" "Keep on as you are, young gentlemen," was the reply; "you're sare to overtake them." "Sas," said a bright Austin youth to his sistei, who was putting the finishing touches to her toilet, "you ought to marry a burglar." "What do you mean by such nonsense'?" "I mean that you and a burglar would get along well together; you have got the false locks and he has got the false keys." Onalie Gina.—" Well, how is your Browning club getting along?" Chicago Girl—"We received his new poem last week.' "Did you like it ?" "It hasn't been read yet. The reading is to take place next month." "Why, 'what causes the delay?" "He forgot to send us the diagrams."— Omaha World. MR. BENTLEY proposed to establish a periodiced publication, to be called "The Wits' Miscellany." Smith objected that the title promised too much. Shortly afterwards the publisher came to tell him that he had profited by the hint, and resolved on calling it "Bentley's Miscellany." "Isn't that going a little too far the other way?" was the remark. SCENE—A fashionable West-End shop. Enter a lady of title, addressing a shop-walker—" I wish to exchange something I bought yesterday." 1 "Yes, madam. Do you remember whether you I were attended by the gentleman with the dark moustache or the gentleman with the light beard?" "Oh, neither I It was the nobleman with the bald head." "MAMMA," said a little girl, "as people get-old does their hair grow quarrelsome ?" "Why no, my child I What ever put such a notion in your head "I thought it must be so, ma, because I heard that old people's hair is constantly falling -out I" A GREEN reporter, in describing a case of what he called "attempted suicide," said: "The poor wretch put a ball through his breast, but failed in his suicidal purpose, although his Wound proved mortal the next rmorning." "FATHER," said a cobbler's boy, as he was pegging away at an old shoe, "they say that the fish are biting good, now." "Never you mind," responded the oid man: "you just stick to your work and they won't bite you." DURING an election, a temperance candidate called upon a turn-Seller and solicited his vote. "I would rather vote for the Evil One himself than for you," was the savage response. "Yes, I know," said the candidate, "but in case your friend should not be nominated, might I then count on your assistance?" A MAN in Pawtucket, It. 1., who tends a rail- road crossing, owns a dog which, at the approach of a train, will seize the red signal flag in his teeth, and running out, vigorously shake it to warn passers-by. As the dog is not liable to get drunk and leave a switch misplaced, he receives us

_ salary. "GERMANY," says the Norristown Herald, "has just discovered a buried forest in her midst, supposed to be ten thousand years old. If the man who lost it had advertised in the Norristown Herald, the chances are that it 'would have been returned to him the same evening. AN inveterate old chicken-thief in Alabama, who had a marvellous faculty for gliding out of a close eorner, was at last caught with a chicken in his hat. He denied the stealing of it, and on being asked how then it got into his hat, he solemnly said: " Dat merster, is jes' what 'stonishes me; but fore de Lord, I 'specs it mus' hab crawled up my breeches leg 1" THE late Sam Phillips, the author of "Essays from the Times," one day met Douglas Jerrold, and told him he had seen, the day before, Payne Collier, looking wonderfully young and well— quite an evergreen. " Ah," said Jerrold, "he may I be evergreen, but he's never red (read)." On my repeating this to Hicks, he smiled and said, "Now that's what I call ready wit.'" ARTEMCS WARD used to tell of an adventure he had in Boston which resulted as follows—"I returned in the horse-cars part way. A purty young girl in spectacles sot near me, and was tellin a young man how he reminded her of a young man she used to know in Warltham. Party soon the young man got out, and, smilin, in a seductive manner, I said to the girl in spectacles, Don't I remind you of somebody you used to know?"Yes'. said she, 'you do, remind me of one man, but he was sent to the penitentiary for steafin' a barrel of mackerel; he died there, t-o I conclood you ain't him.' I didn't pursue the conversation." OF Alexander Henderson, the celebrated divine 1 (the leading clergyman of the Church of Scotland during the early p irt of the civil war, when clergy- men were almost all statesmen), the Episcopalians tell the following traditionary anecdote :—When Charles I. was confined in Carisbrook Castle, he was attended by Mr. Henderson, whoesvas the only divine of the Scottish Church whom this unfortu- nate monarch could ever bear to be in his presence. Mr. Henderson used to entreat that the King would permit him to pray before bin, ; but the King, ! who was extremely averse to extemporaneone prayers, constantly refused that favour, telling 1 Mr. Henderson that he had chaplains of his own, and did not require any other help in the performance of his spiritual exercises. At length the Preshy tei Jan dlviue entreated permission BO warmly that Charles did consent to give him a hearing. Before the commencement, however, of the prayer, His Msjesty eaussd stn amanuensis to take his station behind the arras, aud commit to paper, in shorthand, a correct copy of all that Mr. llenderson should say. This was done; and in the course of a few days, Charles took out a paper from his pocket, and Fending it to Air. Henderson, asked what he thought of this religious rhapsody. "Why," ans wered the divine, after having perused the paper deliberately, " this is a tissue of rank blasphemy." "' replied Charles, "I assure , you, Mr. Henderson, upon my faith as a Christian, ' and my honour as a King, that hi your own prayer 1" Orr course no woman ever did such a thing; t were, that ;brno! suppose now, for the sake of ergument, a that a woman were to go to church for the purpose of showing oil her new Banque, would it be no - religious, so to speak

University College has agreed to accept from Lady Shelley a monument of the poet, whom, like Gibbon, Oxford dons in his day sent down. The monument, which was originally intended for the poet's grave at Rome, ist,the work of Mr. Onslow f'ord, The home of of the .Slielleys is in Sussex,, and the present Lady Shelley is a daughter of the fifth -Mir of Courtown. , : The annual report of • the Liverpool Society,of Painters in Water Colours contains a statement which must be reassuring to aquareliists. The sales of pictures were last year fifty-five, as against eigh- teen the previous year. It may be inferred that trade must have improved, or that the unreasoning I panic against the durability of water-cos, started a few seasons ago, has now Miss Ellen Terry has been credited with many smart sayings. A young offioer, remarkable for his uncommon height, being present a few clays since at one of Mr. Henry Irving's afternoon receptions, I Miss Terry was struck with his appearance, and learned upon inquiry his name and family and that he had been originally intended for the (Church. " Rather for the steeple," was the reply. The tape telegraph misbehaved itself in a some- what happy fashion on Sunday evening 'when it announced that the Prince and Princess .of Wales and Prince Edward of .Saxe-Weimer had attended "diving service" at Eastbourne that morning. Being at a watering-pilace the "diving" service was not in any way inappropriate, though, •per- haps, more in keeping with the Baptist persuasion than with the tenets of the Established' Church.

The Queen's entourage are very arntious to hasten her departure from the Riviera. Since the Court arrived at Windsor her Majesty has visited the Wolsey or Albert Memorial Chapel ,nearly ,every afternoon, and has usually remained thern tor ab4ut a quarter of an hour, engaged in meditation and prayer over the ndffin of the Doke of 'Clarence Mid the tomb of the. Duke of Albany. 'lbis :pracpce is by no means beneficial to the lQueeri's'lialth, and it 1 causes her to be in wretched spirits,•sii it is hoped that she will be induced to start Iforll'Yeres on the 17th.

The , papers amite with tolerable unanimity in announcing the,engagement of Mr. .Alfred Little- ton to Mr. Balfour's sister. .It was so pleasant to say that Mr. Gladstone's nephew is going to marry Lord Salisburfs niece that the <papers recklessly said it •without regard to -fact. The Miss Edith ,Balfour to whom Mr. Littletcn is engaged is handsome young lady, much admired in society, but she is not Mr. Arthur Balfour's sister, and, if her family has any connection with that of the leader of the house it is remote. Mr. ?Littleton, who is rapidly becoming as famous a lawyer as he is a crialfeter and tennis player, lost' his first 'wife, a sisterof Miss Margaret Tennant, in 'childbirth. ;

Mr. Balfour's- sister is; eltretnely intellectual. She is not handsome, but shiis a charming conver- sationalist, and a moat accomplished draughts- woman. While at the. Chietßecretary's lodge she employed her time in landscape painting from nature in the Phcenix-park. Like her brothers she is short sighted, and wears a Tioses-seez. She accompanied her brother when Chief secretary on Us tour through the.congested districts of Ireland, and gave a very interesting account of• her adventures in two papers which appeared in "'Murray's Magazine," which is now defunct.

The great :Nonconformist bodies of London have taken an unusual and significant step. . They have decided to -enter as Christian churches into the arena of the County Council contest. A great meet- ing was held on Monday ..night in the Memorial Hall. It was, carefully stated that its object was not political.nor.to run the caudidatee„of any particular party. But the resolutions of the meeting, pro- posed by such leaders of sturdy. Ndnconformist thought and action as Mr. Guinness Rogers and Dr. Clifford, were a repetition of the main features of the Progressive program, and implied and required the support of Progressive candidates.

Mr. Jesse, Herbert, the e,ble Birmingham lawyer who is invited to oppose Mr. Chamberlain, is a man under middle age, with a small frame, and is much under middle height. He, in fact, without exception, must be the smallest practitioner at the bar. His little.figure is a familiar sightin legal and social quarters in the town. The story is told of him that in some proceedings before a local govern- ing body once he had occasion to object to some- thing or other. ." Yes, Mr.4llerbert," observed the chairman, "your ohjectionlmay be perfectly sOund. But'," he added, in high dudgeon at what he thought a bad breach of professional etiquette, you might be respectful enougt to stand up when alidressing us." And all the time Mr. Herbert had been standing on tiptoe in the earnestness of his objection! , •

His learned friend on the other side curiously enough happened to be Mr. tParfitt, perhaps the tallest man at the bar, standing as he does six feet and a half. He and Mr. 'Herbert literally repre- sented the long and short of things. Well, Mr. Parfltt rose to argue down his adversary's objection. When he had finished; "N'es, Mr. Parfitt, that is all very well," said the sensitivachairman. " But remember please, that because we asked Mr. Her- bert to get-up when speaking we don't expect you to stand on the bench." "I'm not standing on the bench," was the witty ,retort, " but! hope to sit there someday."

The chief incidentin the House of Commons on Monday night was the appearance of Mr. Glad- stone for the 'first time this session. A few minutes after six p.m. a deafening outburst of cheering from the Radicals below the gangway, who were the first to see him as he emerged from behind the Speakers chair, was quickly taken up by the regular Opposi- tion. Mr. Gladstone was looking quite fresh, and had mot the faintest trace .of that fatigue which would leave its thee in far younger men who had made a lengthened journey from earlyimorning over land and sea. He wore a white carnation embedded in maidenhair in his buttonhole, and conversed joyously, sitting between Sir "Wm. Rarcourt on one side and Mr. John Morley on the other.

The bronze statue of the Duke of ,Connaught, which Kr. George Wade has just ;finished, and is now to be sent out to Hong tong, is pronounced by the Duke and all others who have seen it to be an excellent likeness ; moreover, it is one of tbe most artistic works that have issued from English studios in recent years. The statue was commis- sioned by Mr. Chator to commemorate the occasion on which the Duke opened some important public works in Hong Kong. It is rather more than life- size, and represents the Duke, in undress general's uniform, standing in an easy but graceful attitude. Royal personages are not, as a rule, good subjects for a sculptor, but Mr. Wade has certainly been very successful in producing a statue which combines a high degree of "actuality.' with still higher artistic qualities.

Mr. Ford Madox-Brown's studio was thronged on Saturday afternoon by a company .of admitting friends, who came to bid farewell to the artist's latest achievement," The Opening of the Bridge- water Canal," before its departure for the north. This fine and decorative work, with its richly refined colour and intense originality of design is the eleventh (and last but one) of the series commissioned for the Manchester Town Hall; it is also one of the most strikingly successful. Mr. Madox-Brown, whose luxuriant silvery locks and grandly-modelled features seem to belong more to the fifteenth century than to thosefinde siecle days, received his guests with the dignified, and yet wholly simple and genial, manner so peculiarly characteristic of him. He was assisted in his hos- pitable task by his daughter, Mrs. Wm. Rossetti, and her husband.

(FRom - - • ) The death of Miss Clough, the Principal of Newn- ham College, which took place on Saturday, will seem to many people to mark the close °Elbe first chapter in the history of women's univeraityiedu- cation. Miss Clough was one of a little band who were enthusiastic in the cause of higher education for the sake of education. "The Principal," as she was always affectionately called, delighted in bring- ing within the fold of the College the poorest, and socially the least-fortunately placed girls. It was 'her pleasure to stretch the capacity of scholarship, exhibition, and loan funds to their utmost, to afford these penniless young women the knowledge that their minds craved. And when their education was complete to the furthest point that Triposes can attain, she then 'sent the students forth to be- come teachers in their turn of other students. Miss Clough, who was as everyone knows, sister to the poet, came of an old Welsh family, but spent some of her early days in Liverpool. Almost as soon ,as she grew up she took to teaching, and on leav- ing Liverpool she started a school for boys and girls together, where Mrs. Humphry Ward was one 'of herpupils. Later she began to organise lectures for women hi Manchester and Liverpool, Professor Stuart delivering :one of the earliest courses. It was considered' a wild scheme, when Professor Sidgwick,Mr.Favicett, Professor Stuart, and one or two others had the courage :to suggest that ladies , might as, well come to the lecturers in Cambridge ~as lecturers go to the ladies. However, reason was on the side of the scheme, and it grew. , , Then a house had to be taken for the students who,flocked to Cambridge—pretty old Merton Hall. But they grew too many for it Newnham Hall was built. Then another, and yet, another block of buildings was added, uhtil at last there stood the splendid women's college at which strangers marvel. Miss Clough presided over one hall, Miss Gladstone; the vice-principal, over another, and Miss Lee, the Sanskrit scholar, over the third. In recent years, when the responsibilities of her post had begun to tell upon her, Miss Clough was assisted by her neice, is Thena bough; tbe poet's daugh- ter. 'though Said to have been plain as n girtiffies Clough was extraordinarily picturesque in old age. ,She had. masses of hair of brilliant white, from be- neath which Hashed dark eyes of h singular depth and fire. She had a strangely mobile mouth, which was seldom is repose. Hence it was difficult to 'give her expression in a portrait. A picture was painted of her some years ago by Mr. Richmond, but not being considered altogether a success, she satlately to Mr. Shannon for the fine picture which now adorns Clough Hall. It is certainly largely dud- to' her caution in steering clear of possible diffi- culties, to her 'care not to offend Mn. p-rundy. and 'to .her tact ,in dealing with students, that a revolu- tion has been acdomplished in Cambridge without arousing any hostility.,

div.head: TILE UNKNOWN PAINTER.
div.p: TILE UNKNOWN PAINTER.

Murrill°, the celebrated artist of Seville, often found on the canvas of one and another of his pupils unfinished sketches bearing marks of rich genius. They were executed during the night, and he was.utterly unable to:conjecture the author. One .morning the pupils had arrived at the firtuclio before him, and were grouped together before an easel, uttering exclamations ,of surprise; when Murrill° entered. His astonishment was equal to theirs on& finding an unfinished head of the Virgin, of exqui- site outline, with many touches of surpassing beauty. He appealed first to one and, then to another of the young gentlemen, to see if any of ' them would lay claim to it .; but each returned a sorrowful negative. "He who has left this draw- ing will one day be master of us all," said Murrill°. ' " Sebastin,', said he ton youthful slave that stood trembling by, "who occupies this studio at night?" "No one but myself, signor." " Well, take your station here to-night, and if you do not inform me of 'the mysterious visitant to this room, thirty lashes shall be your punishment on the morrow." The slave bowed in quiet submission and retired. That night he threw his mattress before the easel, slept soundly until the clock struck three. Re sprang from his couch and exclaimed, "Three hours are my uwn, the rest are my master's'!" He seized a brush, and took his seat at the frame, to erase the work of the preceding night. With brush in hand, he paused before making the fatal stroke. "I can- not, oh, I cannot erase it 1" said he.; ' rather let me finish it I" He went to work,a little colouring here. a touch there, then a soft shade; and thus three hours 'rolled unheeded by. A slight noise caused him to look up. Murrill° with his pupils stood around ! the sunshine was peering through the casement, while yet the taper 'burned. Again he was a slave. His eyes fell beneath their eager gaze. "Who is your master, Sebastian'?" " You, Signor." • "Your drawing master I mean ?" " You, Signor." "I have nevergiven you lessons." "No, but you gave them to those young gentlemen,and I heard them." "Yes, and you have done better: you have profited by them," Turning to his pupils he said, "Does this boy deserve punishment or re- ward, my dear pupils?" "Reward, signor," was the quick response. "What shall it be?" One suggested' a'suit of clothes, another a sum of money 4 but no' chord was struck in the captive's bosom. One said, "The master feels kindly to-day ask your free- dom, Sabastian." He sank on his knees, and lifted his eyes to his master's face "The freedom of my, father !" Murrill° was touched, and said: "Your pencil shows that you have talent; your request, that you have a heart. You are no longer my slave, but my son. Happy Murrillo! I have not only painted—l have made a painter." There may still be seen in classic Italy many beautiful specimens from the pencils of Murrill° and Sabastian.

div.head: HOW BRUIN GOVHIS HEAD FAST.
div.p: HOW BRUIN GOVHIS HEAD FAST.

A party of hunters en the Florida coast came suddenly upon a bear prowling about a beach. and gravely inspecting such articles as were brought up by the waves, which were richer than usual in plunder from the fact that that there had recently been a severe storm. The author of "Wild Sports in the South "thus describes Bruin's treatment of such wreckage: He would first look at an article, then smell it, touch it with his paw, and finally, after deliberately seating himself, with his hind legs projecting in front, turn his head on one side, and try to crack his new acquisition with his teeth. The burlesque gravity of his manner was indiscrib- able. He threw away a cocoanut, as being too hard to chew, ate an orange with great satisfaction and presently discovered a small cask, which he en- deavoured to open. By dint of much biting be en- larged the bunghole, so that he could insert a paw; then beheld the cask on one arm, and kept the other ,paw busy in rapid journeys thence to his mouth. But this method of getting at the contents did not satisfy him, and presently, standing erect on his hind feet, he inserted his nose in the barrel, and then his head. Now a bear's nose is so sharp that it goes through a small place very easily, but owing to the heavy folds of skin about the neck, and the fact that the hair and ears are set backward, it (low, not possess the same facility for coming out. Bruin was fast. He began to pull back, but as he pulled, the barrel came with him, and as he rolled on his back, pawing ineffectually at its convex sides, it anerely revolved about his head, as if it were,on a pivot. Then alarmed by the sound of our laughter he took fright and ran, wearing the cask on his head like a helmet. Up the hill he rushed, lost all sense of direction, and rolled head over heels squarely among us. Picking himself up, he reared, and began growling and waving his paws, but was speedily released by one of the negroes., who broke the barrel with a blow from his club, and scattered the mackerel with which it had been filled. The bear rewarded him for this service with a blow of the paw which laid him on the sands, and in another second was himself stretched there by the discharge of two rifles.

• iIXAM IN Eft, SATURDAY, TOIL STRANGE SEA. WAVE. -- Occasionally therenppears a great wave ,eping across the calm surface of the ocean in the ,fairest weather, and when no wind is blowing. There are few perils of the sea more to be dreaded than such a wave. Fortunately they are very rare, yet more than once a ship has encountered one. Only a short time ago the Etruria was met 'IV a wave of this kind, which rolled upon her like a wall of water, and breaking against her sides, swept the deck with irresistable force, killing one sailor and seriously in- juring others. A smaller and less staunch vessel might have been overwhelmed and sent to the bottom by the blow. The cause of these singular waves is be- red to be some disturbance of a volcanic nature at the bottom of the sea.. Volcanoes exist in the ocean as well as on land; in fact, nearly all the vol- canoes known are on or near the sea coast. It is easy to see that an upheaval at the sea bottom may start a billow at the surface of the water when we remember that huge waves have been sent clear across the Pacific Ocean to San Francisco by volcanic shakings of t'ae earth an the borders of Asia. The world under water is not only three times as exten- sive as that which is covered only with air, but it possesses many of the same great natural pheno- mena on a scale which is perhaps proportionately vast, but of whose existence we are made aware only by such indications as the volcanic ocean waves that ships occasionally encounter

div.head: 'THE WESLEYAN PRESIDENT AND THE BISHOP OT TRURO.
div.p: 'THE WESLEYAN PRESIDENT AND THE BISHOP OT TRURO.

- • The Rev.. Dr. Stephenson, President of the Wes- leyan Conference, preaching at St. dust, Cornwall,, on Monday evening, referred in strong terms to the remarks made by the Bishop of Truro after avecent confirmation service at St. Just Church. There Was,! said Dr.Stephenson,sometimes a feeling ofdeolation and consequent depression in churches in remote districts; but if that was the case wish the St. Just' Wesleyans, let them remember they belonged to a great Church. The Bishop of Truro told theni they were good people but mistaken, and earnest but, misled.' What most impressed him about the bishop's remark was its impertinence. Who was the bishop? A: hard worker who had attained to an hoiwurable and responsible position; but in the matter of scholarly attainments his whole body was not as thick is the little finger of .Dr.Moulton,the speakers immediate predecessor in the tpresideney.' The bishop's attainments dioj.not entitle him to speak of Methodists in that insolent way. So long as they did 'God's work and kept theiespirituar light burn- in, there was little fear of their being mistaken or misiled. The Methodist Church was the largest in the world, and had attained that honourable position within a century and a half. The Church of England had intimated a desire to promote Christian unity end receive the Methodists into their fold. Methodists also desired unity, but, be- ing the larger Church, they claimed to do the ab- torbing.

div.head: SMOKE-CONSUMING KITCHEN RANGE.
div.p: A SMOKE-CONSUMING KITCHEN RANGE.

A kitchen range which economises fuel to the extent of 50 to 70 per cent., which consumes its own smoke, and which is efficient in cooking and baking, and in its hot water supply is an article worth having in every kitchen if passible. These and some others besides, are guaranteed in regard to the " smoke consuming and fuel economigng kitchen ranges" .(Marsh's patents) 'which are supplied by Messrs. Baxe,pdale and Co., of Miller-st., Manchester, whose advertiAment appears in another column of this paper. The people best qualified to speak as to the merits of the range are, of course, those who have used it, and from these there is a flatter- ing list of testimonials. The " idea "of the inventor was that if the smoke from the top of the kitchen tre were .prevented from going straight into the lines and-so out of the chimney top, and could be persuaded to go downwards through the fire, not only would the smoke nuisance be so far got rid of, but it would contribute to the bulk ,of the fuel Used; and what is now passed off as unconsumed fuel, called " smoke " would give all its combustible materials for ,the production of heat. This, we are told, is what Marsh's patent does, and does very effectually. Not only this, but, while it used to be considered necessary, in order to make a brisk cooking or baking fire, that "best house" coals should be used, by this fireplace, such expensive coal is quite needless. The cheap "slack " and " smudge " actually do better work. One user of the range writes that, as to smoke, there is none at all in the kitchen and very little is to be seen issuing from the chimney, and only when the fire is first lighted or mended after being allowed to go nearly out. Then there is a slight curl of transparent smoke to be seen for a few minutes only—after that ,nothing. Another user writes " your claim of a saving of 30 ta 50 per cent. in the cost of fuel,l believe to be rather under than over 'the mark, and the range has thus further great advan- tage—that, while with care it is surprising how little fuel is really necessary, yet it is almost impossible to make it waste." A. Rabaghati, M.D., F.R.C.S., Ed., writes that "on the whole I think the improvement effected by Marsh's patent smoke-consuming fireplace is such that its economy is certain to ensure its introduction into general use, and that the saving of the labour of looking after the fires, and, above all, the vast improve- ment they will probably effect inthe health of thepeople will be more than commensurate with their economy."

div.head: RUNCORN WATERWORKS COMPANY.
div.p: RUNCORN WATERWORKS COMPANY.
PROPOSED EXTENSION.

The half yearly meetineof the shareholders of this company was held in Runcorn Public Hall on Monday evening. Mr. John Brundrit, J.P., chair- 1 man of directors, presided, and there were pfesent I MeSeltd. John Simpson, Wm. Whittaker,Wm. Hayes, W. D.Jelliffe, James Collier, W. F. Salkeld (sec.) and W. Jones (assistant secretary). The report stated that the revenue account showed a balance of £992 7s. 3d.,including £245 335. VI. brought from tbe previous halt year, out of which the directors recommended a dividend to be declared at the rate of five pounds per centum per annuum, free from income tax., parable on and after the first day of April next : this would absorb £750, leaving a balance of £242 Ts. Zd. to be carried forward. The repairs to the Runcorn Engine had been completed to the satisfaction of the directors, and the engine had been at work continuously for several weeks, and went very well.—The Secretary having read the certificate -of the auditors (Messrs. Robert Foulkes and James Collier), the Chairman moved the adoption of the report and statement of accounts. He Said he did so with greater pleasure than he had done previously, because the directors might fairly congratulate them- selves and the shareholders on having a °otter report than any yet issued. The accounts showed a larger balance, after paying all expenses, than they had ever had, and at the same time showed that the salaries and expenses for coals and other things were slightly less ; a fact which was proof that due economy was used, but the improvement in the receipts was owing naturally to the large increase in the population and works in the neighbourhood. He trusted this was only the stepping- stone to future progress, and that at the next meeting they would have to announce an even more satisfac- tory state of affairs. All the machinery and plant was in very good order and unless something unusual occur- red, would not require very much attention for some time to come. With regard to the water supply it was quite sufficient for the existing population, bet it might not be sufficient in twenty years or so. He wished them to understand that there was no scarcity of water; there was plenty for present requirements ; but looking to the future and the prospect of mere works being established through the Ship Canal, and other sources, when a much larger supply of water would be required, the directors had thought it prudent to take time by the forelock and be prepared to meet such a contingency, which would contribute to the further success of the Company. On these grounds the directors were now in correspondence with the Company's engineer, Mr. Efawksley, perhaps the most eminent authority on water in the country. At present the subject was only in an embryo state, and when some- thing was conclusively arrived at, to provide further supply, the directors would take an early opportunity of bringing it before the shareholders.—Mr. Hayes seconded the motion.—Mr. Jolliffe pointed out that the deprecia- tion fund had got down to £l5O, and he suggested that £lOO of the surplus should be put aside towards replac- ing pipes which must be gradually wearing out.—The Chairman replied that they might have paid a larger percentage than they had, but they had kept that bal. ance so that some of it should be put to the reserve fund. They hoped with watchful economy to be able to fnrther increase the reserve fund. The Company I was now in a stronger position than before.—The motion was carried unanimously.—Mr. Jolliffe proposed a vote of thanks to the Chairman and the directors.—Mr. Collins seconded.—Carried.—On the motion of Mr. Whittaker, seconded by the Chairman, a vote of thanks I was accorded the secretary, and Mr. Salkeld, in reply, said he and Mr. Jones would continue to use their best efforts for the success of the company.

• A. TALI WITH NA.1717:.. ' A ' -I wish to sit with Nanny Wictdrington for half an hour, Mrs. Moor, but there is not the least need for you to wait! You can go on home, and send back Alice, and try that time I shall be ready to return." Mrs. Moor promised to make Alice, Lady Caller- ley's maid, aware of her mistress's wishes; and not sorry to be /herself released from further 'attendance, the good woman gursued her way tal one. "Now is my chance," murmureb Silna, " De) 1 is safe dowsvonder, in the dancing room, and the 'old woman as Alone. Surely she will tell me this mysterious secret concerning -the Callerley family? I know there is one. I can it in thp,uir all around use, :even if there had never been hint given to VOX me with vague conjectures. It 00411- mg me—killing me! Yes, strange as it seems, I am dying if a secret, because-s-ah, not because I am- mirious, but beca.u`se it keepsone from being one in soul with my husband !" Old Nanny was not by any means in the most gracious-of tempers. She was losing her boy, the one who teased and tormented her, and therefore the eneshe cared the most sabout. He was bright and merry, and told her funny things about folk— things which were too often not quitetrue, but tverehone the less entertaining for that reason. He whistled like a blackbird,-and had a laughing face and twinkling eyes that aseminded her of a certain fisher lad who had madepassionate love to her more than seventy years ago, but whose leatuiles 'she remembered much moresviviclly now than those lot the husband in whose company a long life had afterwards been spent. :For the sake of this far off love of hers she grudged little Ailsie iCarr a win- some bridegroom. Bell was a good girl 'enough, but then she .had , the one stipreme fault of being •a gith , A i,sAipktilar to note how very little estimation someavomen hold their own sex in. Maternal love, if :A exists in them at all towards their daughters, •eAsts as a very calm and feeble sentiment; 'while towards their sons, on the contrary, it -is a perfect passion. Old Nanny was thus constituted. Bell might wait on her hand and foot, as the,saying is, and -yet the old woman vissuld•feel no sort of gratitude/ because "Bell would niver be nowt 'but a lass while one blink of Bill's merry eye would delight Nanny)beyond all measure, and a few careless words 'of kindness from him would fill her for the day with supreme content. Besides her discontent at the marriage of het:. favourite, ;there was the minor, but very present grievance, that fun was astir, and that she was out of it. Very few people are content to eat their cake, and then live on the memory of that feast. It is a great pity but that the appetite would diem natural death at the same period. of, time that the cake comes to an end. But to keep on getting hungry without any means of proeuring more cake.; or worse 'still, to have a store of nuts without any teeth to crack them, is, it must be confessed, very hard" lines indeed. Pqr Nanny! She was a wicked old heathen; and nothing wonld ever make her the sweet, subdued, contented, mellow creature one reads of in good books, and meets alas, so seldom in real life Every woman who has rus- ticated for close upon a century, and who has ex- perienced nothing of wicked ways ,appertaining to a city, is not necessarily either innocent or idyllic. There are old country women who prOduce upon one the same sort of impression—quaint, fresh, rhythmical—as do some long disused out-of-date psalm and hymn tunes. One associates all sorts of • old-fashioned, homely things with them; sprigs of dried lavender, laid amongst deliciously cool, clean linen; beds of sweet Smelling herbs, and bushes laden with fair white roses; a big Bible, with a faded flower, plucked by the fingers of a long dead' lover, or a downy yellow ring of hair from the head of some baby, since grown old and grey, placed between its leaves, to mark some dearly loved passage; a passage, be sure, containing a promise, not a denunciation; a blessing, not a curse. Nanny Widdrington was not such a one as these. Yet the same hand made ravens and hawks as fashioned doves and singing birds. And it was not merely the sweet and gentle portion, but the whole of His work, that He looked at and pro- nounced good. It was not the most propitious moment Lady Callerley could have chosen for her visit. Nothing, at first, would the old woman talk of but her own grievance. How was she ever to do without Bill? He might have/ waited a year or two longer. It could not be Many days now before his( old granny would be dead and gone. But young folk were all selfish alike. Cuddy was courting too, they told her, and a widow woman with six bairns, no less, to say nothing of her being a Methody body, and setting her face against the lad siding a good stroke of business. And as for Bell,--s "Has Bell a sweetheart also?" asked 'Silvia, interested at once, "but of course I know she must needs be loved Only Ido not think any of the men down in the village are good enough for her. She is a wonderful beauty. If she had been born a lady, -what a fuss they would have made of her I" •

"Handsome is as handsome does," replied Nanny, crossly, "if she had done right she wadn't ha' leaved me all by myser while she went jiggin' and gallivatm' 'off be weddin's !" This was very unfair of the 'told thing, since she herself had insisted upon Bell's going, and would also insist upon having every 'detail of the day's proceedings recounted on the girl's return. Be- sides, she had not been left alone. A fishwife from the village had been keeping her company until a few minutes previous to Lady Callerley's advent, and Bell was certain to be in very soon.

"His she a sweetheart? ' repeated Silvia. "Oh, ay, ye needn't ask! Aw'se warrant it'll no be lang or she'll take wing too, and leave th' aad 'nu alone! But he's a darin' chep and a plucky one, an' aw'll not Fay but what she might do Worse I" " Who is het "
"Nay, my leddy, aw'm not just at liberty to tell ye that I Ax the lass yersel' if ye want to knew. There's them aboot that would fain catch hold on him ! "

"He'll have a beautiful wife, and a good one!" "Hoots, ay! The lass is weel enough. But ye didna' come to crack aboot her, did ye?" "No," said Silvia, slowly and hesitatingly. "Do you remember something you 'once said—it was the first time I saw you, I think? You told me that if there was anything I wished to know about the Callerleys, I could not do better than apply to you." Nanny nodded. Her beady eyes twinkled with the foreknowledge of mischief to come. " WoU, now I want you to keep that promise," went on Lady Callerley, with growing eagerness. "There is something they hide from me, and I must know it—l , must I tell you!" . .

Nanny watched her intently, as her finge. twined and untwined themselves with restless force, and her lips .grew tremulous, and her eyes big and round. Lady Callerley was evidently a nervous, excitable subject. How the old woman often longed for such a listener, when it was in her to paint the horrible and the grotesque. It was really too bad that the simple pleasure of frightening a lady to death was a debarred one. It made her feel sulky and malicious. "Why don't you speak, you horrid—no, you dear old 'oman? Don't pretend that there is no secret—no mystery ! I feel it. I knew there was one from the very day I came, when I asked Lancelot about that stone by the water, and he would not give me the history of it. Do tell me, I am one of the family, and I oiwht to know I" .

"Vilatten story is this ye want me to tell ye?" asked Nanny, with malicious slowness. Silvia would have liked to have taken her by her skinny shoulders and given her a good shaking. "Oh, you know, you know quite well! I see it in your wicked tantalising looks I" "Darrsay ! Ma wicked looks, indeed! Aft' what for dinna ye ask yer goodman, sin ye're so curious about family matters?" Silvia flushed, and made no answer. CHAPTER XIX. THE CHURCHYARD ON THE MITT.

Towards the close of summer there are often grey, sad, cheerless days, which, in their hopeless apathy, have an infinitely more dispiriting effect than all the glooms of winter. They are out of season, and consequently unnatural. Through all the sunny hours that follow they strike a chill; in the same way that a sudden wailing minor chord, breaking through a buoyant dance measure, keeps vibrating for long afterwards upon the ear of the dancers, and drags the time in the joyous allegro succeeding it. Days like these are forlorn with prophecy, and heavy with dread.

• At' the close of such a day Lady Caller_ley wandered alone in the old churchyard on the cliff, and thought of the weird stories she had heard about it. It was certainly a " dowly " , spot tAi choose when clay Was dying, but the girl had now melancholy fits occasionally, and it suited with thorn exceedingly well. Standing upon a crumb- ling sandstone cliff, which jutted far out to sea, the ruined church of Callerley, with its clustering tombstones, formed a picture of desolation and de- cay difficult indeed to rival. A windowless gable; a porch unroofed and tottering; walls more than half fallen to the ground; gravestones displaced and sunken.

Year after year the storms of winter whistled through the sacred edifice and wind and weather httd been allovied to:work edifice, will there, no human hands interposing to or save it. Year after year the great waves itldthundered and battered away at the cliff upon which it was built, scooping out the soft stones, and gradually undermining the place of the dead. Year after year the sea crept further inland and with greedy, open mouth, swallowed up a little more of the space intervening between church and precipice; and ere long the shaken battered walls themselves 'would certainly sink beneath the waters.

It was a sort of siege. The" living element stormed the fort with the columns and phalanxes of its mighty army; and what were the defenders to withstand it, but merely the bones of dead men? Like battering gams came it, ponderous waves; and like spears and arrows were hurled its foam and spray, and the terrible winter storms; and the rain and wind helping it, stripped from the dead their primary wrappings of earth, and laid upon them instead wreaths of shining brown and olive sea-*eed. • It was a albge that must necessarily be anceqsahu In the end. They, the invaded, would soon all lie deep down under the sea. "They shall lie low, dead brother by brother, in a place that is radiant and fruitless, and the folk that sail over their heads in violent weather shall come down to them, haply and all they shall lie there, together." How was it that Silvia Callerley, the little laugh- ing beauty, who ought by rights to have lived in the sunshine like a bright summer butterfly, came to choose this eerie spot to wander in at such an hour?

Ever since the talk with Nanny Widdrington, the place had possessed a strange and potent fascination for her. And she was no longer the bright careless beauty of six months before 1 Her face was growing sad and wititfnl, and there was a frightened look in her blue eyes. It did not therefore seem any longer strange that she should choose to linger there, and read the records of past generations. Lichens and mosses were creeping over the in- scriptions, and obliterating. the words graven upon the headstones; as though intent upon effacing the piously phrased falsehoods, or the meek inanities that have ever been thought fit and proper for tombstones.
Why is it not held cruel to say false or ,stopid, things about those who can no longer contrad;c:. them?

- "Are they all good people who die?" muse Silvia, dolefully, "What becomes of the poor ners, I wonder? Ah, here is a headstone that hold itself upright still, as though proud of a just 11 eminence. Let me see what it says :

•0! let us on her image dwell, A soul transporting spectacle, On whom even angels gaze, 4 A pious saynte matured for God, She's shaken off her earthly clod.' "Oh what a dreadfully enlogistic concerni, hope that Lancelot will not consider such nee necessary ahout nie, if I die! Ah, this looks better.. ','Short was my Vine, 1 Thellonger be my rest, _ . Cod took me hence, He judged it best.' "yes, that is good. Not a word of praise. - remember that, if possible , Some of the quaint epitaphs with their naulgiwa 9f mundane and pious matters brought a smile, even Lady'Caller/ey's sd mouth. Such -was thoii, one _ upon the landlord of. the " Golden.. Goose " Breamish, deceased a short time pievionsly. "The landlord of the Golden Goose . Has flown aloft, fledged and let loose. Submissive to the Heavenly will, . The son keeps On the business still." The touth of advertisement in the last line was Irresistibly harnorous, and appealed to Silvia at So did the one about thirty sailors belonging' t° the .Avondale, which ship was wrecked and Wee' f. to pieces upon a dangerous ridge of rocks outside of Frenchman's, By, raj little tot the south of Breamish village. One after another their bodies had btiert cast ashore and buried in one comma; grave. It was difficult to decide whether the tear was to be dropped for the pour dead sailors, or for DavY Jones the cheated'? , After wandering aimlessly' about for some tinn; Lady Calleiley began to • grow tired, and the so"- monotony of the.. scene and the hour affected her Spirits. The House adjourned at seven o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS, THURSDAY. _ . .

The SpeWei-tO-octhe chair at three o'clock. QUESTIONS &c.—. The Manchester, Sheffield, and Lin- colnshire (extension to London, Scc.) Bill and • the Blackpool Improvement Bill, were read a second time. Sir M. Hicks Beach informed Mr. Samuelson that no County Councils had availed themselves of their powers to make advances in aid of the emigration or colonisa- tion of the inhabitants of their districts. The Attorney.' General, replying to Mr. Addison, said he could not under take to initiate any legislation, this session in regard to the Vexatious Indictments Acts; and Mr. Balfour indi- cated to Mr. Conway that in the present state of business it would not be useful or possible to introduce a measure to relieve elementary scHbols from the 'pressure of local rates. Further questions had reference UP responsible government in Natal, the military forces in Burma!), and pensioners and the Post Office. Mr. MACNEILL complained strongly about Mr. Curzon not being in his place to answer questions on India affairs. COI7RSII OF BUSINESS.—MF. BALFOUR moved a resolu- tion that the House should meet on Tuesdays and Fri- days at two o'clock, and that the principal business at snch morning sittings should be financial business and proceedings on the first introduction and reading of bills. Mr. GLADSTONE said he should be disposed to assent tp the motion if its operation did not extend beyond Easter. After some discussion the resolution was carried by a majority of 222, subject to Mr. Gladstone's suggestion. SUPPLY.—The House went into Committee of Supply, and the Mombasa Railway scheme gave rise toa long and animated discussion; in which Mr. Gladstono took pare. He strongly complained of the absence of information on the subject, and exenapted himself from every jot and tittle of responsibility for the undertaking. Mr.Labou- chere was speaking at midnight when,the debate stood adjourned. s The Labourers'(lreland)Allotments Bill passed through Committee. The House adjourned at a quarter-past twelve.

div.head: DR. HOUSTON ON WORKING CLASS QUESTIONS.
div.p: DR. HOUSTON ON WORKING CLASS QUESTIONS.
THE EIGHT HOURS DAY, ALLOTMENTS, AND

OLD AGE PENSIONS. On Saturday evening the Albion Lodge of the Association of Iron and Steel Workers, which is composed of workmen employed at Messrs. Monks, Hall and Co.'s works, held a knife and fork tea at the Workingmen'd Mission, Bank Quay, Warring- ton. There were 71 members present at an enjoy- able repast. After the tea a meeting was held at which r. Houston, Q.C., the 'Liberal candidate for Warrington,attended by invitation. Dr. Houston was accompanied by Mr. W. Pierpoint, and Coun- cillors J. H. Fleming, and H. Roberts, and Mr. J. Clayton (Liberal agent.) The meeting was pre- sided over by Mr. Arthur Birch. The CRAntmett remarked that some of them 1 thought that a social gathering of the members of their trades union would be a very good opportu- nity of hearing what Dr. Houston had to say on questions relating to labour legislation, especially las Warrington was a local. centre, and a great pop- don of the electorate were working-men. The ques- tions upon which they should like to hear Dr. Hou- ston's opinions were, first, as to the payment of members of Parliament. Then there was the ques- tion of an eight hours, day, a rather ticklish question to deal with, because they were not all unanimous, but he certainly thought that miners and chemical workers and all those engaged in unhealthy or hazardous employments, should have an eight hours day. (Hear, hear.) As they felt theit way, and saw that it was capable of being adopted in other trades,he hoped those who represented them in Parliament would further such Acts as were brought before the Legislature. The other questions he had to put were relating to allotments for town workers, and also to compensation for brewers. (Hear, hear.)

pa. HOUSTON'S SPEECH. Dr. HOUSTON laid it gave him great pleasure to be amongst them that evening and to address an assembly of working-men in a social and a sociable manner, and not as if he were making a regular and formal speech. There were a large number of questions before the pub- lic at the present day which very closely and intimately concerned working-men, and he should have been glad if upon that occasion he could have covered the entire ground, but it was impossible. He should, however, take the occasion to deal with every one of the ques-1 tions which interested working-men in the course of that campaign. (Hear, hear.) There was one question which their Chairman had alluded to which he could dispose of in a moment, and that was the

COMPENSATION or BREWERS. He should give them none—that was the simple answer that he gave, and he did not want to elaborate that further. (Applause.) He did not consider they were entitled to any compensation. (Hear, hear.) With regard to the

PAYMENT OF MEMBERS, that was one of the most important question that work- ingmen had to consider. If a man was ambitious 'to serve his comtry as a member of Parliament the present system necessitated the expenditure of a substantial sum of money and a substantial sacrifice of income, and the first result of that was that the choice of a constituency was necessarily narrowed. He dare say there was hardly a man that was present who did not know of some I thoughtful, earnest, sagacious, highminded and eloquent man that h i e would gladly see n the House of Commons, but that was excluded from that position by the present system. He could illustrate that. He thought that according to the general opinion of the public, the Irish Parliamentary party contained within its limits a very large proportion of men who were posseseed of the qualities which'were necessary to make men successes in the House of Commons. A proportion. of those *ere paid members, and they were members who could never have occupied the position they did but for thei fact that they were paid members, Mid?' the loss which Ireland would have sustained by omission and exclusion of these men froth, the ranks of the ' Irish Parliamentary party would ' have been simply incalculable. (Hear, hear.) That showed them at once the great advantage the payment of members would be to the community, and the loss which is sus- tained by the present system excluding from public life a large number of men who were eminently qualified for it. (Applawie.) If members were to be chosen upon, their merits and not upon accidental circumstances, it appeared to him the prlnciple of the payment of members must be recognised. (Hear, hear.) The next matter.he had to refer to was the

div.head: QIIISTION OF EIGHT HOIMS.
div.p: QIIISTION OF EIGHT HOIMS.

He wished he was able to give them as clear and de- finite an opinion uponthat subject as he had been able to give them upon the first subject he had touched upon. AS their chairman had observed the ,working classes themselves were not unanimous upon that subject, and he had always been of opinion that the first thing that a practical politician ought to do was to inform himself of the opinion of the class more immediately concerned. (Hear, hear.) He himself had no so much confidence In mere theorisation. He liked to come to close quarters, and to ask the people who wear the shoe where the ihoe- pinches. That question was still but in its infancy and they must not be in too much hasp, and they must not be asking people to make up their minds in a hurry upon an importapt,question of that kind: 'Up to the present: the workingmen themselves were not •unanimous upon that subject, and therefore, standing in the position of an outsider, seeing in a Sense " through a glass darkly,", he must try to fall back upon

FIRST PRINCIPLES and see how he might obtain guidance and direction from the principles which ought to guide them in the conaider- ation of the subject. Let them think for a moment of <me Or two of the natural limitations of the hours of labour. 'There'Were three in which he thought almost all people 'ought to concur. In the first place, the hours of labour ought to be limited so that there should be what he should call no waste, because if they unduly extended. rthe how% of labour they would defeat their:own object. ' When the hours of 'about+ were unduly and unnecessarily eittended the prodtict bore no proportion to the amount of tithe that was to be given to it, but, on the contrary, very, often .. the very opposite result took place. The bowl. of • labour should not be extended beyondtthat point at which the maximum amount of produce can be secured. That was -.14 mach in the interest of the em- ployer as the employe: (Hear, hear.) The next consid- eratidn they had to take int 6 account 'Was of the greatest importance, and that was that the hours bf !pour Should be so limited that the health of thewprkeirs shOuld not gaffer. (Applause:) He need hot elaborate that; it. was perfectly obvious, and the legislature, he was happy to say, was prepared to act upon that prin- ciple. (Hear, hear.) The third limitation—and when he said limitation his was speaking of the goal at which they ought to aim, because it was a most important thing that in practical politics that they should have a definite object in view, that the height which they were looking to ,reach should be a. clear definite point. (Hear; hear.) The third limitation was this, that the working- man should have a reasonable leisure for recreation and self-trilproveitient. (Applause.) He did not say there might not be other limitations that they ought to loOk forward to, but ha thought tic' had :defined' the, ttrlee , Wtiich were the Most important and which Were; im- mediately at all, events, the "most material. -Therefore, the questimi they had to consider was how thosalimita- .laotiOXlX

RAILWAY SERVANTS, and it did appear that the legislature would be quite en- titled and quite capable of interfering in the case of rail- way servants, and say that they should not work beyond a certain nuMber of hours, not simply in their own in terests but in the interests of the community whose lives and persons were imperilled by the overwork of persons who) require to be always on the alert and to have their wits and senses about them, which they could not have if they were over-worked. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Those were illustrations. The question arose, could the State interfere beyond that, and if so, how far? He was greatly afraid the answer must be that the State could not safely interfere beyond those cases in which the evidence was dor and the case beyond a doubt. After that point had been reached it would lie with the working- classes themselves to work out and solve the problem which primarily concerned themselves, but which also concerned the public at large to a very great degree. It had been suggested by some that •

A MINERAL RIGHT HOURS IDLY should be fixed upon by the Legislature, and that no working-man should be entitled to work beyond eight hours. He had considered that question with some care, and he was bound to say that there 'appeared to be in- superable difficulties in the fixing of such a day. If they were a nation that were isolated from all the world, a good deal might be said in favour of that, but the manufacturers of this country depended not simply upon the home markets, but upon the markets of the world, and unless international arrangements of that kind could be made, how were they to prevent the com- merce of this country being diverted from its present chanaels to different channels? Unless foreign countries were prepared to fall in with that view, and were pre- pared to limit their hours of labour to the same number of hours which were fixed upon in this country, how were they to compete with the foreigner in the foreign markets? He must confess, he did not see the answer to that. The only answer which could possibly be saw-, gested—and it was an answer to a certain extent—was that they should endeavour to get the foreigners to fall in with their views on that subject, and to similarly re- strict the hours of labour. But, of course, that could enly,be done after a considerable period had elapsed,and very considerable advances had been made in organisa- tion and in international legislation, and, therefore, for the present, at all events, he could not see that it was possible for the legislature to interfere by the hard and fast rule of imposing an eight hours day without com- pletely disorganising industry in this country, the con- sequences of which were not easy to foresee. But he did not despair of seeing the hours of labour very largely educed. He had the grextest confidence in the

POWER OF LABOUR ORGANISATION. It had achieved great results hitherto. No doubt the number of trades organised and the number of peqple organised appeared up to the present to be a very small proportion of the number of trades and the number of workers, but the principle of organisation was spreading every day, even amongst unskilled workers. (Hear, hear and applause.) They might have to wait a EORSi• durable time before anything like a general organisation of labour came into existence, and he had no doubt that, before a very long period at all events, the time would arrive when the majority of workers would be organised in some form or another, and when that took place they would really have that question in their own hands, because they could themselves from time to time work out the problem in their own particular trade, and in trades cognate to their own, and he thought the result would be that, in the long run, if the hours of labour were not reduced to the point to which they should all wish to see them reduced, yet at all events they would be reduced to reasonable limits. (Applause.) With regard to the

QI7ESTION OF ALLOTMENTS he was glad that an interest was being taken in it by a non-agricultural comrpunity. It would be a mistake to suppose that urban communities were not interested in the question of allotments. He dionot see why mem- bers of urban communities should not have allotments as well as members of agricultural communities. (Hear, hear.) He hailed with satisfaction every agitation brought forward in favour of the creation of such hold- ings, and he did not see why there should be any diffi- culty in compulsorily purchasing land in the neighbour- hood of towns. He held that th 3 working-man in the town was quite as much entitled to consideration as the working-man in the country, and therefore any system of alletments which did not provide for allotments for persona employed in town labour was an incomplete system. (Hear, hear.) He had been asked to say a few words on the question of
OLD AGE PENSIONS. (Hear, hear.) That was certainly one of the most im- portant questions which had been brought under the notice ot the public and the lapouring classes of late

Tifet first Idea &tit wild 12 occur in all minds was , ",,Fthistavis ON stYpritVt:- and of course, in a sense, the regislatui4 Was' er- ful and could effect ,any object whic t really placed before it, but they. were met with diffi4dities. Take the most important of the three liMitationg—the health of the workers—and consider for a moment whether the legislature was a body capable of determining that ques- tion. They were at once met with this consideration, that they must discriminate between different occupa- tions, because what was not a severe pe=iod of labour for one class of workers might be a very severe and very excessive period for another class of workers. (Hear, hear.) Taking the most exhaustive and the most dangerous class of employment at the one end of the line, and going down to the other end et the line, they would find a series of gradations So line that he thought it would be perfectly, impossible for the legislature to draw aline at any particular point. It could, however, make wide distinctions and clear distinctions, and it could say that the labour of such an occupation was of such a character, and of such severity, as was calculated re impair er at all events imperil the health of the work- ers; and that the workers in that particular employment should not'be occupied more than a certain number of hours in the day. (Hear, hear.) That, he thought, the legislature could do, and, as the chairman had referred to the , OCCUPATION OF mums, bethought it was perfectly possible that the legislature might say that the daily labour of the miners should not extend beyond a certain number of hours. (Ap- plause.) And so in those employments in which chemi- cals were produced, employment naturally deleterious to health, the legislature could take steps in a case like that and say that it had been clearly shown to them that the health of the persons employed in that occupa- tion would be endangered and would be imperilled by a greater number of hours in the day than was fixed up3n, and therefore in the interests of those people and in the interests of the community, labour should not extend, beyond that period. (Hear, hear.) Again,there were cases in which the safety of the community was involved such as the case of

The monthly meeting of this Council was held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday evening. The Mayor. (Alderman Greenall) presided, and there were also present Aldermen Francomb, Holmes, Chandley, Wright, Sutton, Harrison ; Councillors R. T. Fair- dough, Shaw-Green. Smethurst, Tinsley, Hill, Muir, Ashton, Flood, Beaman, Monks, J. Fairclough, Roberts, Hepherd, F. A. Roberts, Dixon, Garnbe, Heaton ; Messrs. Whittle (town clerk) Longdin (borough surveyor); and Chorley (borough • trea- surer).

a wood pigeon, from the School of Art, on the recommendation of the Technicalgustructim sub- Committee it was resolved :-1, That schohtrilllN be given on the result of the examinations according to scheme submitted as follows : A scholarship, value 53. or 103.' fl respectively for a nst class, elementary or ad- vanced, in science, and 10 elementary and 5 advaanced scholarships in art, equal in value to the evening class fees for the session ; 2, that the examination fee be paid for all candidates in commercial examinations whose names are sent in by the teachers; 3, that classes be provided for elementary teachers nominated by the Cheshire Technical Instruction Committee, that Commit- tee paying the following amounts :—Drawing up to 15 students 20 lessons, £lO ; cookery, up to 12 students 24 lessons, £2O: agriculture up to 16 students 20 lessons, £lO ; 4, that Warrington teachers be admitted free,under the usual conditions, to the agricultural class. Councillor H. Ronswrs moved the confirmation of the minutes. The MAYOR asked if the Committee had taken into consideration the advisability of opening the Museum and Art Gallery on Sundays, or whether they wished to bring forward a motion on this subject at the next meeting of the Council. , Councillor H. ROBERTS replied that the Committee had ' not yet had an opportunity of considering the question, and as it would be largely a question of expense, the Committee had deferred it until the next year's estimates came before them. The Committee did not consider they were carrying out their duties until they provided a supply of daily papers, and in the event of the estim- ates permitting them, they intended having a supply of daily papers. (Hear, hear.) The Committee also hoped to lay aside sums of money in order to acquire pictures of credit, and especially works of Warrington artists. It was a curious fact that the Corporation did not possess a single work of art of any ef the able and distinguished artists yet living who had commenced their careers in Warringtcn. The minutes were confirmed. CEMETERY COMMITTEE. At a meeting of the above Committee, it was reported that the receipts for the past four weeks amounted to £B2 3s. 9d., against £BB 2s. Bd. in the corresponding period of last year. The ensuing year's expenditure was estimated at £621. On the motion of Alderman HARRISON the minutes were confirmed.

div.head: MARKETS COMMITTEE.
div.p: MARKETS COMMITTEE.

At a meeting of the above Commmittee it was stated that the total income from all sources for the past four weeks was £262 Is. lid. ; corresponding wriod last year, £259 Is. lid. ; increase, £3. The estimate of ex- penditure was £1,719 4s. These minutes were confirmed, on the motion of the MAYOR, seconded by Councillor BLACKHURST.

THE GAS WORKS STAFF.—THE PRICE OF GAS. The Gas Committee reported that the average illumi- nating power of the gas for the four weeks preceding February 19th was, at a meeting of the above commit- tee, reported to be equal to 18.5 candles at both works. The following resolutions were passed :—That on the resignation of Mr. James Cooper as cashier, Mr. W. S. Howard be appointed cashier in his place, at a salary of £l5O per annum ; that Mr. Cooper be employed in the office at a salary of 353. per week; that the salary of Mr. E. J. Smith be increased from £9l to £lOO per annum, and that an additional ledger clerk be engaged at a salary of 20s. per week. Alderman Iloo.iss moved, and Councillor R. T. FAlR- =vox second.d, the adoption of the minutes. • Councillor DIXON expressed a wish that the re-arrange- ments of the staff mentioned in the minutes had been left over till the end of the municipal year. Councillor SMETHURST thought that the Council ought to have a distinct understanding that applications for increases of salary should not be made every two years by officials. He considered that it was about time some steps were being taken to reduce the price of gas or tly• meter rents. (Hear, hear.) Out of a total of 54 towns, there were 45 largo towns where the price of gas was lower than in Warrington. Councillor H. ROBERTS expressed his satisfaction that the Gas Committee had been able to re-arrange their staff with positive advantage, and also with being able to economize to the extent of £39 per annum. He was pleased to observe that two of the younger servants of the Corporation, who had served their time in the ser- vice of the Corporation had thus been offered an oppor- tirnity of improving their positions. He sympathised with every remark which had been uttered by Councillor Smethurst with regard to the price of gas, but they should not forget if they paid 40s. for what was worth only 20s they could only expect a corresponding result, This town would have to bear the burden of the fact that it paid for the gas works" through the nose." It was possible to produce gas as cheap as any town in Lancashire but it was the capital expenditure which handicapped them, and he was afraid it would do so for generations to come. Councillor Snew GREBN said that about a month ago. when the Council were discussing the merits of several applications for advances of salary, he suggested that there should be a maximum sum to which an official could ultimately attain. He thought that the present occasion would have been a favourable opportunity for making such an arrangement. Alderman CHANDLET said that in the event ~of the introduction of any such system he would strongly op- pose it. • Alderman HOLMES said the Committee had had the matter of reducing meter rents under their considera- tion for some time, and they hoped soon to be in a position to bring forward a matured scheme, (Hear, hear.) The minutes were then adopted. PRECAU rIONS AGAINST FIRE. —TEIE PRICE OF

div.head: WATER.
div.p: WATER.

The Water Committee had passed resolutions that all the fire hydrants in the borcugh be regularly and sys• tematically inspected, and in times of frost that provi- sion be made for the hydrants being kept ready for use; further, that the next rate be levied for three-quarters of a year, from 25th December, 1891, to 29th December next, and that discount be allowed to all owners of cot- tage property whq pay the same before the 28th Jane next.

Alderman Faastcomis, in Mbving the confirmation of the minutes, said he was pleased to inform the Council that by the end of the week they would have inished laying the main from Horsemarket-et. to the Fire Engine Station with Appleton water. They had also laid three fire hydrants since their last meeting. Re- ferring to some criticism as to the price .of water, he said they had had an expenditure at the Water Works of about £274,000,and as a committee they were most anxious that when twelve months had elapsed they should be able to show that they had bought a paying concern, and not a losing one. (Hear, hear.) Every member of the Council would agree with him, and also with the committee, that it was not wise to tamper with the prices of the water. (Hear, hear.) They were most anxious to make the greatest possible use of the water for the manufacturers of the town ; but if one or two people wanted them to make an excep- tion in their case, the committee would have to seriously consider Wnether it would be wise at the pre- sent time to do so. The only information he had upon the subject was for the quarter ending 24th September last. They had then 18 consumers by meter at a shilling per thousand gallons, and those people used 1,792,300 gallons, which brought in a revenue of £9O 12s. 6d. That was for Appletou water alone; 13 at 9d. used 17,005,400 gallons, which brought in £647 ss. ; one consumer at 6d. consumed 4,211,000 gallons, bringing In £lO5 ss. 61. There was an erroneous idea prevalent that they were pouring water into the river at the rate of 600,000 gallons per day. They were certainly pouring a considerable amount of water into the river to waste, and he should be pleased to see it turned into the sewers. (Hear, hear.) But, as they understood, Appleton water was not laid on all over the town, ,and they had to be - careful in laying the pipes ; otherwise they would have an enormous increase of the rates. They tried. their best to so put down the pipes conveying the Appleton water that they would be able to sell a consider- able quantity of surplus water, and to produce a large revenue. For the time he had referred to they used 23,000,000 gallons (he left out the odd figures) of APPle- ton water which was 255,653 gallons per day. They had 600,000 gallons to go at, and they had now got 344,350 gallons to dispose of. But they Were not in a position to dispose of it until they had pipes laid on to the various works and to the houses of people who were likely to be consumers. As far as the Winwiclt water' was concerned, they had BO consumers at a shilling per thousand gallons, who used 3.000,000 gallons, -and gars them a revenne of £l7l 12s. 4d. ; nine consumers at d. who used 9,500,000 gallons, and brought in £358 ; and four consumers at 61., who used 19,500,000 gallons, at a cost of £429 Os. 9d. ; so that it would be seen that there was a large surplus of water. They were trying their best as a Committee to meet their consumers, but they did not want to show a loss rather than a profit at the end of theyear, (Hear, hear.) Councillor SHAW Gmeest said that in some towns there was a water rate levied upon the ratepayers, which materially assisted the revenue of the Corporation, and enabled them to set their water cheaper than they.could in Warrington. Alderman Suwon was' glad te hear that the Water- works were going to be a profitable investment. Councillor BLACkFIVIZST referred to- the need of fire hydrants in Latchford, and Alderman Francomb pro- mised that the Committee would take the matter into consideration.
