-of the world. We have frequently argued in these olunans that a general reduction of the hours of labour—which would be good alike for employers and employed—sheuld be made upon an interna- tional basis to ensure its permanency; and we aro pleased to notice that the Liberal candidate takes pretty much the same view. He said: "Let them get foreigners to fall in with that arrange- ment. But that could only be done after a con- aiderable period had elapsed, and a considerable advance had been made in organization and in international legislation." Happily the workers of all countries are beginning to realise that they have common interests, and that they have too long been held asunder by statesmen who have kept up race hatreds by playing the game of war. International movement is slow, but it is sure, and they pace will certainly be accelerated as organise- -141 is perfected. Before concluding, Dr. HOUSTON touched on the question of allotments, and Pointedly remarked that he did not see why pro- vision should not be made in this respect for Working-men as well as for agricultural labourers. It is a matter of course to say that a speech so thoughtful and reasonable was well received; and Ir 6 are quite sure that it will be equally will appre- ciated by our readers. Dr. HOUSTON has alreadyl ,:sadered a serviee to the electors educationally ; llt will rest with them ere long to decide whether 40 shall render still greater service as their repre- : Waittative in the House of Commons.

TEE advance of civilisation is not Tooth And Claw. an advance pure and simple from the brute to the angel. So far is this from being the case that there are some who .c'entend that there is just as much sin and suffer- 41g in the world to-day as " when Adam delved • Eve span." In their view it is as it was in the beginning, is now, and ever shall be—cruelty with- out end. For instance, a civilised man puts ivory t°a great many uses. It is certainly an admirable loaterial ; and frequently adds a grace .to home life as a means of adornment; but it is not plea- lent to know that is is directly associated with • 1017 and murder. Petty wars are waged in Africa, and whole villages depopulated, for the lake of securing stores of ivory. Mr. Stanley %themes that every pound of the coveted article that reaches this country represents the loss of 11,bulnan life. Thus, we have the ivory cross as 'no emblem of peace at one end, and the crimson e°rse at the other. It is much the same with Other things. It is the fashion for ladies to adorn their bonnets and hats with the wings, plumes, atid feathers of birds. But what a sacrifice of life it involves! It ought to give pause to the lovely creature in the lovely hat to learn that to pro- Core the humming bird which adorns her head- Der eight Or ten humming birds have in all pro- bability been sacrificed. The same holds good as to the oriole, the king-fisher, and the egret, " counting in the young who die of starvation, the Wounded which fly away to drop down and die in the woods or among the reeds, and those which are mutilated and destroyed by the pellets so inuch as to be unavailable for purposes of decor- ation." There are some women who take these things into account and refuse to be party to this Wholesale slaughter ; but, with the majority, fash- len is everything—the holocaust is nothing. Women are not of course alone to blame. There 4ftre Men who go out with gun and " murder- iis-11141g eye" to shoot somethieg—just because it in! fine day. What can be pleasanter at a water- e„lPlace than to watch the movements of sea- With their swift, broad and beautifully ' ;aped wings And yet to some people the chief P2easure of the thing consists in killing or maiming °le birds that happen to fly near the shore. Some- thing has been done in this country by the klforcement of the Wild Birds Protection Act ; 1311 t there is still room for the cultivation of more Inunane sentiments, especially amongst the young. At Southport feeding the sea-gulls is one of the 4ights of the winter season. This is done as an evahibition from the jetty at the end of the pier. Weave o'clock is the hour fixed, and a few minutes before the time the birds—some hundreds in num- her "may be seen coming in flights from afar. 'unger is a sharp thorn, but is it hunger alone that %tables them to guage the time so nicely ? What 4 rhsh there is of wings when the whistle is hoard 141-1 the first piece of food is thrown in the sea. i The . air s vocal with their cries ; while the way in ...Which they wheel, and circle, and poise, and dart the very poetry of motion. The man with the °Wline-piece is not permitted to exercise his laltirderons skill, or he would be there for that per- rsle undoubtedly. It is a beautiful and unique ; and yet it has a drawback ; the " scramble" r each piece of meat—twenty darting to seize /vh t • Et is merely, enough for one—is an object les- see • in the struggle for existence which is too sug- ;▪ rive of "nature red in tooth and claw" to be kte°llY agreeable. Indeed, although the sea-gulls Pretty to look at, they behave no better in this ZPect than creatures of the stock exchange— ° refined vultures who Steal by night and steal by day, Doing it all in a legal way, •Ile they scream in praise of civilisation. This strange world.

div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."
Under pressure on our space this week, we have had to hold over various items of news, &e.

If, as expected, the Ravenhead Schools are per- manently closed, St. Helens will be brought face to face with the question of providing a School Board. And why not 1) It is the custom in the few be- nighted towns where no such Boards exist to ex- press horror at the proposal. A hundred years hence, there will be horror at the recollection of such stupidity.

Referring to the Tory candidate for the North- wich Division, who hails from Blackburn, the "Blackburn Times" says:—" By the way, it is an open secret that the Duke of Westminster will 'stand all ex's,' so Mr. Whiteley may well look for- ward to the amusement of giving Mr. Brunner as good a run for his money as was ever seen in that part of the country."'

The Germans are thinkers, and sometimes they act as well as think. On Tuesday the Reichstag refused to vote the money desired by Government for the construction of cruiser corvettes. What if refusal to flad the supplies for warlike purposes were to become contagious? Really, there will be hope for humanity when Parliaments hesitate to increase the military burdens under which so many nations are staggering.

It seems that the workhouse inmates at Watford were treated to a magic-lantern entertainment the other week, and they enjoyed it very much. An offer was made to give a similar entertainment, but it was declined because the day selected was Ash Wednesday t The chairman, backed by a clergy- man, thought the day " unsuitable." So the poor inmates are denied a night's enjoyment becanse the Watford Board is particularly wooden.

The Lord Mayor of London is letting it be seen of all men that he is a Welshman. He presided, on Saturday night, at the annual Welsh National Banquet ; and, on Monday, he attended in state the Welsh Festival, in St. Paul's Cathedral. He is quite right in keeping his country and his coun- trymen in mind. Welshmen have been snubbed so much in the matter of honours that the Lord- Mayor's attitude will be something towards re- storing the balance.

The Rev. Thomas Wetherall, rector of Stocking Pelham, Herts, was charged at Much Hadham, on Saturday, with trespass in search of game. It was proved that a hare was started and was killed by his dogs when he was out with them. After hearing the defence,the bench convicted and fined defendant 303. Poaching on preserved sermons is no new thing on the part of parsons of a certain type. But poaching for hares—well,—the rev. gentleman must be a bit harum-scarum.

With regard to the impending coal strike, there seems to be a disposition in some quarters to con- demn the miners for standing out against a reduc- tion in their wages. But they are quite within their right in seeking to sell their labour at the highest rate. They are not ov3rpaid now for the work they have to do. And, besides, the matter in dispute is small relative to the total price of coal. Why not seek to knock something off royalty rents instead of colliers' wages?

What is the matter with the Primrose League? If it is not exactly going to the dogs, some of its paraphernalia is to be had dirt cheap. A cor- respondent sends us two Associate diplomas which he picked up in Warrington market. He fancied the frames, and got the two for ninepence—the diploma; signed by the " Registrar," and bearing the" mark of the Grand Councillor," being thrown in. We understand that the two Associates are still "on the list ;" for there must be a show of membership whatever becomes of the members.

How is it that Councillor Bolton, after being adopted by the Conservatives to take the place of Mr. John White as a County Councillor for War- rington, has had to step aside for Mr. Lewis Voisey ? It is true that some Conservatives made uncomplimentary remarks upon the selection; but what of that? William got the start; and it is rumoured that he was not at first disposed to give way. How is it that he has xissed the rod so meekly ? There was a time when he sought to make people believe he was an " Independent" ; but now those days are over ?

By-the-bye when are the County Councillors for Warrington going to follow Mr. W. R. Earp's ex- ample and give an account of their stewardship ? It is surely due to the electors to say what they have been doing on their behalf during the past three years. Now that Warrington has a popula- tion exceeding 50,000, the question is sometimes asked—why should it not become a full-fledged County Borough? Is it better to leave things as they are, or is Warrington in this, as in many other matters, lacking in spurs to prick the sides of its intent?

The death of Mr. William Sharp in a foreign land touches a chord in every heart, for it adds to the sadness of the event to think of a journey for health and pleasure terminating in illness and burial a thousand miles from home. It would seem that he was not strong enough to endure the great change from the heat of the day in Egypt to the cold at night, fo; he was subject to chest weakness. Luxor, where he was interred—separated from friends "by mount and stream and sea "—is a vil- lage on the eastern side of the Nile which is noted for its ruined temples, and as occupying part of the site of the aneient city of Thebes.

Whilst the Tory candidate for Warrington is recruiting his strength in the Mediterranean, the Liberals are vigourously pursuing the cam- paign upon which they so auspiciously entered when they selected Dr. Houston. Every meeting thus far has been characterised by great enthu- siasm. Owing to the Public Hall being engaged, it has not been possible to arrange for a meeting in that building until April 13th, when Mr. Herbert Gladstone, M.P. will attend, and sup- port the Liberal candidate. Mr. Thomas Burt, M.P., the working-men's representative for Mor- peth, has promised to attend a subsequent meet- ing, which will also be addressed, it is expected, by the Earl of Aberdeen.

The Warrington Musical Society had an unfor- tunate experience, on Tuesday evening, in having from causes beyond its control, to make so many changes in its programme. There can be no ques- tion that the element of uncertainty which was introduced had some effect upon band and chorus; and thus prevented a repetition of the big success which was previously scored. The Princess Ahmadee was disappointing; the audience ex- pected to tear a first-class vocalist as well as see a pretty Princess. But what then? There are high tides as well as low tides. Mr. Crossley as con- ductor, is doing his work well; and the public gust go to the next concert in the full assurance that such a fortuitous combination of unfortunate circumstances caxnot happen again.
LADY _DERBY'S EYBSIGHT.
The Courtess of Derby underwent most success- fully an operation for cataract performed on Tues- day, at Holwood, in Kent. Lady Derby is progress- ing very satisfactorily.
THE BLUE HUNGARIAN BAND.

The opening concert by the Blue Hungarian Band was given in the Winter Garden of the Liverpool Naval Exhibition, before the Mayor of Liverpool (Mr. J. de Bela Adam) and he Mayoress, and a very large and representative audience. The well-known band has hitherto in its visits to Liverpool met with a deservedly enthusiastic reception. Under the conductorship of Herr Berm, the band played a pleasing and varied programme at the initial per- formance. Whether they are playing their own native airs, selected from the operas, or other pieces more or lees known to English ears, the remarkable fact remains that their natural retentive memories, extraordinary power of producing any air they may have heard, added to a natural musical talent, are alone responsible for their performances. Indeed we believe that many members of the band do not know a note a f music. The band gives four different concerts during the day. They will remain at the Exhibition until March 12, and are to be followed by the Ladies Pampadour Band.

div.p: UNIVERSITY EXTENSION LECTURES AT RUNCORN.
In Bethesda Lecture Hall on Monday evening, the Rev. W. Hudson Shaw will lecture on "Machiavelli."
ALBERT-ROAD _WESLEYAN CHAPEL, WIDNES.
The members and friends of this place of worship spent a pleasant social evening together on Tuesday night.
PHOTOGRAPHY. To a good audience at St. Ambrose Church Mission Room, Mr. G. Warner on Thursday delivered a capital lecture on the above subject.
WESTON BIBLE AND MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT CLASS.
At the usual weekly meeting of this class held on Mon- day night last, a paper was given by Mr. J. B. Clarke on " Hymns and their Writers."
HOLY TRINITY BAND OF HOPE, RUNCORN.
An entertainment in the schoolroom on Monday even- ing to a good audience and an enjoyable evening was spent. The Rev. Dr. Preston presided.
BETHESDA BAND OF HOPE, RUNCORN. A miscellaneous entertainment was given by the mem- bers of this society on Wednesday evening to a good audience. The Rev. J. Sampson presided.
THE FARMERS' AUCTION COMPANY.
This company have declared a dividend of 5 percent. for the past year. The turnover was .£8,679 103. 6d. The subscribed capital of £250 is still intact. BRUNSWICK WRSLRYAN BAND OF ROPE, RUNCORN.
The monthly meeting was held on Monday under the presidency of Mr. E. Marshall, and a miscellaneous pro- gramme was gone through by the young people.
CRTJRCH BAND OF FIOPE, RUNCORN.
A capital entertainment was given in the National Schools on Tuesday evening under the presidency of Mr. Worthington. There was a numerous audience.
LECTURR BY MR.
H. WADE DEACON,
AT WIDNES.
In connection with the pleasant evenings at the National Schools, Mr. Deacon on Thursday evening de- livered an interesting lecture on "A peep through the microscope."

COMMITTRI) FOR TRIAL. Yesterday, at the ‘Vidnes Police Court, Win. Dodd, of Birkenhead, was committed for trial on a charge of hav- ing wilfully broken a pane of plate glass of the shop of the Public Benefit Boot Shop.

WIDNES FREE LIBRARY. During February there has been an attendance of 14,302 in the reading room an increase of 979 on the corresponding month last year, 5,469 books had been issued from the Lending Library an increase of 383. Messrs. Deacon, Robinson and Sadler have been appoint- ed to co-operate with the General Purposes Committee of the LOcal Board in the erection of the new Technical Schools. GREENWAY ROAD BOARD SCHOOLS, RUNCORN. . . .

Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress illustrated with a large number of magic lantern slides, formed the chief feature of an entertainment given to the scholars attending these schools last Friday evening. An interesting and instructive description ef the various scenes as they were thrown on the screen, was given by Mr. J. T. Looney. At intervals during the entertainment the hearty singing of a large number of sacred songs, the words of which were thrown on the sheet, rendered the evening more enjoyable. The amusing story of the "Pied Piper of Hamelin" was next illustrated. This part of the programme was a source of intense enjoy- ment to the juvenile audience, and the frequent out- bursts of laughter and applause fully testified to this fact. Mr. E. W. Rosser gave the descriptive reading. A very pleasant entertainment concluded with the singing of "Abide with me," followed by the National Anthem.

RUNCORN TONIC SOL FA CONCERT. In connection with Runcorn Tonic Sol Fa Choir, the third concert of the seventh season was held on Monday evening, and it is pleasing to record that the enterpris- ing efforts of this local musical society, succeeded in attracting, not onlv a large, but an. appreciative audience The choir, which as usual was admirably conducted by Mr. John Holford, G.T.S.C., the hon. conductor, rendered several choruses and part songs in fine style ; .• Moon- light" and "Day break " being especially enjoyed by the company. Mr. Frederic Owen was in capital voice and with appropriate force and expression he sang "Deep in the mine," and " Out on the deep" and was recalled for each song. Miss Moulsdale, who has a sweet expressive voice, contributed "My lady's bower" and "Sunshine and rain," and well sustained the reputation that she has gained with the Runcorn people. Mr. John Child (Carl Rosa Company) made his first appearance on a Runcorn platform, and by his singing of Let me like a soldier fall" and "Star of Bethlehem" he raised the audience to a high pitch of enthusiasm,and encores were vocife- rously demanded. In conjunction with Miss Mousdale Mr. Child also sang the duet "Oh, Maritana," a splendid performance, and the two artistes were re-called and bowed their acknowledgements. An encore also re- warded Messrs. Child and Owen for the duet "I am King of Spain." The instrumental portion of the concert was much enjoyed. Miss Nunn, L.R.A.M., brilliantly performed several pianoforte solos, and her sister, Miss Gordon Nunn, charmed her auditors by her perform- ances on the violin, an intrument of which she showed a I thorough knowledge and command, and she was en- cored on each appearance. A highly enjoyable and in- teresting cocert was brought to a close by the National Anthem. Mrs. W. P. Kay fulfilled the duties of accom- panist with her usual efficiency. UMBRELLAS REOOVERED.—J. and W. Durrox, Sankey-st., Warrington.—.Adet. FRODSHIM COUNTY COUNCIL.

In this division the contest is void of any strong feeling. Mr. Slater Lewis has held meetings at Norley, Kingsley and tielsby, and last night held one at Frodsham. Mr. Baxter held a meeting in Frodsham Town Hall on Thursday evening. All the meetings have been well attended. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-at.. Warrington.—Advt.

THE 60AL DISPIITE AND THE UNITED ALKALI CODIPA.NY. Considerable uneasiness has been experienced by those employed in Runcorn and Widnes, through the United Alkali Coy., having posted throughout their works, notices to the effect that in conse- quence of the strike of colliers, it might be nec.es- sary toclose or partially close their establishment. In both towns householders experience much diffi- culty in obtaining coals for home consumption, and the prices have risen 3s. a ton. UMBRELLAS RECOVERRD.—J. and W. Durros, Sankey-et., Warrington.—Advt. MR. T. C. EDWARDS Moss, M.P., AT WIDNES. The annual tea party and concert in connection with Widnes Parish Church, was held on Shrove Tuesday. Mr. T. C. Edwards Moss, M.P., presided and in the course of a speech, said the members of the Church ot England must be ready to defend her when the occasion arose, and urged his hearers to take advantage of the many social and moral rceans for improvement offered by the Church in Widnes. A capital concert was given by a num- ber of local vocalists, and the proceeds will be devoted to repairing the Church which has been damaged by the recent storms. UMBRELLAS RECOVF.RED.-7 . and W. Durrell, Sankey-et., Warrington.—Advt. WARRINGTON BANKRUPTCY COURT.

At this Court, yesterday, before the deputy. registrar, Mr. Ridgway, Henry Cragg, junr., builder of 7, Heath-lane, Penketh, and carrying on business in Bewsey-st., Warrington, underwent his prelim- inary examination. In reply to the assistant official receiver the debtor said he commenced business in 1889, with a capital of .£6O and last year took a shop in Warrington. He attributed his failure to losses on a contract to build a new class- room for a Baptist Chapel and to bad trade. His account showed a deficiency of £lB2 4s. 7d. The examination was adjourned, and the examination of George Booth, butcher, 83, Greenway-road, Run- corn, was closed. BASSIXETTES. aarland, Ironmonger, Warrington and , Earlastown.

(15T SATURDAY, MARCH 5, 1892.
RUNCORN COUNTY COUNCIL ELECTIONS.
THE DAY OF DECISION.

To-day, the struggle which has been proceeding for the past three weeks in Runcorn North, will be submitted to the arbitrament of the popular vote, and the claims of the contending parties be decided at the ballot box. The issue is more important than at first sight may appear. It is not merely between two estimable individuals but whether Runcorn North shall be represented on the County Parlia- ment by a gentleman of avowed Liberal prin- ciples, or by an Independent Conservative, as a member of Major Hazlehurst's committee has des- cribed that gentleman, and also whether the Libe- ral party is to be broken up and divided by the de- fection, of a few so-called leaders. The workera on each side show that a cry of independence will not bear a more than superficial examination. The two camps are clearly and iharply defined into Liberal and Tory, and if Major Hazlehurst has the good fortune to win the seat to-day it will be put down as a Tory victr,ry. It is for working-men to consider whether the party who have for genera- tions striven hard to obtain for the masses of the population their just rights and demands are more likely to administer the laws in the county for their benefit, than the party who have always acted as the drag on the coach of progress, and as the defenders of class privileges. If the electors of Runcorn north are wise, they will, in the secrecy of the ballot box, vote for Mr. Ockleston, a man who is in keen sympathy with Ow people and who believes in. and will act on the principle, that the nation's safety depends upon trusting the people to the fullest extent, both in the making and adminis- tering of the laws of the country. The arrangements for conducting the election have been completed by Mr. John As.iton, the re- turning officer. There are to be five polling stations in the National 13chools in Church-sr., and the poll will commence at 8 a.m., and continue to 8 p.m. Immediately after that hour the ballot boxes will be conveyed to the Court Room at the Police Sta- tion, where the counting will take place, and it is expected that the result will be declared about 10 p.m.

THE TEMPERANCE PARTY AND TOE CONTEST. The combined temperance organisations of the town have issued a circular to tho electors, in which they point out how probable it is that the County Council will be made the licensing authority of the county, and draws attention to the fact that Major Ilazlehurst is against the direct veto or local option, and in favour of compensation. The electors are urged to vote for Mr. Ockleston, the Licieral candidate, who will be guided in his action by the direct veto.

div.head: MR. OCCLESTON'S CANDIDATURE.
div.p: MR. OCCLESTON'S CANDIDATURE.
MEETING AT MILL BROW.

In support of the candidature of Mr. Wm. Ockles- ton, a public meeting was held in Mill Brow Board School, on Monday evening. There was a large at- tendance, and Mr. Alfred Norman presided. Amongst those present were the candidate, Dr. Hodgson,C.C. (Crewe), Mr. J. F. L. Brunner, C.C. (Sandbach), E. Wynne Humphreys, T.Lea, D.Bisbrown, L. M. Tem- perley, E. unison, John Withington, Thos. Riley,W. Cartwright, T. Clegg, John Hitchens, S. White,John Jones, W. Handley, and John Clark (secretary). The CHAIRMAN said Mr. Ockleston in his address was sound in most of the points they wished pressing for- ward, and therefore it would make thein views appear weak if they declined to support him as a Liberal. Major Hazlehurst came forward as an Independent can- didate, and yet admitted his Conservatism, and, there- fore, on that ground they could not support him inas- much as he did not come before them on straightfor- ward grounds. Major Hazlehurst said there were no politics in the Council, and when he went there he left them behind. Fle the Chairmrn) considered that his principles were part of himself, and he must take them with him, and if he were called upon to exercise them they knew the way he would go. He considered there were at the present time

POLITICAL QUESTIONS IN THIS COUNTY, • but in the future there would he many more, for the powers would be increased when the next Glad- stonian Government came into power. (Applause.) , He was sorry to think there were some gentlemen, in the middle classes, who professed Liberalism, and still their action in the past few days had shown WANT OF PRINCIPAL AND STRA,- NESS.

div.head: ;KLESTON
div.p: ;KLESTON
THE LIBERAL CANDIDATE.

The above is the portrait of Mr. Wm. Ockleston, the Liberal candidate for Runcorn North, in the election for Cheshire County Council, which takes place to-day. He is 31 years ot age, and is a few months the junior of Major Hazlehurst. the In- dependent candidate. Mr. Ockleston's ancestors settled in Runcorn early in the present century. and his grandfather became the proprietor of the tannery in Halton-road, which had been formerly worked by Mr. Wright, and which was known as the Old Tannery. On coming of age, the candidate's father was taken into partnership, and, under his management, the business was removed to the pre- sent premises, Halton-road Tannery, which had been built on the most modern principles and adapted for the quick system of tanning, and of very much larger dimensions than the old one. The late Mr. Wm. Ockleston was a man of great energy and ability; the business prospered exceed- ingly ; and the works are now conducted by his two ' sons, John and William, with increasing success. Taking a great interest in the public life of the town,the deceased gentleman was a member of the Board of Commissioners, and was the head of the Liberal party. In the election of 1868, he took a prominent part in support of the candidature of the late Mr. G. W. Latham, against Mr. J. B. Lister Warren, now Lord De Tabley, who was backed by the Egerton family interest. In fact Mr. Ockleston laid the foundations of the present undoubted Liberalism of Runcorn district. In accord with his political convictions, he always took the side of the people in all public matters, and in the Water- works controversy of 25 years ago he strongly ad- vocated that the Waterworks should belong to the Commissioners as the local authority, but unfortu- nately for the present generation his views did not prevail. When he died about 12 years ago, he left the two sons previously mentioned, and William, the candidate, is a firm believer in his father's principles. Although but in his early manhood, he has for some years evinced a desire to take a part in public work; but up to the present time has not coma prominently before his fellow townsmen. Since the formation of the North wich Division Liberal Association in 1885, Mr. Ockleston has been one of the vice-presidents,and has helped the cause both by his purse and his active interest. He was one of the promoters of the Runcorn Liberal Club, of which successful institution he is the treasurer and one of the trustees. He is a Liberal of what

may be called the advanced type, and is a firm believer in the aphorism that the people's will shall be the nation's law. lie is not is very ready speaker, but the practice he has had during the present con- test has considerably improved him, and there are not wanting indications that he will become an effective expounder of the faith that is in him. He has youth on his side, and if given the chance will become in the future a valuable public servant.

div.head: .R. WILLIA
div.p: .R. WILLIA
AN UTTER WANT OF PRINCIPAL AND STRAIGHTFORWARD-

That was enough to fill right thinking people with con- tempt. (Applause.) There were gentlemen who Might appear on the Liberal Council in the South Division, who appeared there perhaps for objects best known to themselves, and they found them in the North Division professing another thing altogether. He had received

div.head: LETTER FROM MR B RUNNERM.P. _
div.p: A LETTER FROM MR B RUNNERM.P. _

It read as follows:—" Druid's Cross, Wiavertree, Liver- pool, 29th February, 1892. My dear Norman,—Please receive my hearty thanks for the earnest work you are doing in the cause of good overninent, both local and imperial. No question has been more discussed of late in Cheshire than what is called the introduction of politics into local affairs. My observation of the man- agement of local affairs for many years, and over a wide area, has convinced me that the principle is a sound one. (Applause.) In the first place, you get better men to offer their services, in the second, you get a much larger number of voters to take an active and intelligent inter- est in local government, a most important matter. And lastly, men elected by the party organizations attend to their duties far more regularly than the non-politicals. freely allow that the occasions for a party vote in the County Council are very few, but, on the other hand, they are very important, and on these rare, but impor- tant occasions

div.head: LIBERAL WILL VOTE RIGHT
div.p: THE LIBERAL WILL VOTE RIGHT

and the Tory will vote wrong. (Applause.) On these grounds, I approve of the management of local elections by the party, and cordially wish you success. (Applause.) Mr. Ockleston's record up to now is an ample guarantee that he will devote himself heartily to the service of his constituents, we want men in the County Council who are in favour of the un- restricted control of the police by the elected representa- tives of the people. (Applause.) Men who are against the employment of the police as cheap gamekeepers. (Applause.) Men who will keep an eye on the charities— (hear, hear)—and see that they are

MANAGED FOR THE GOOD OF THE PEOPLE, and not for the benefit of the parson. (Applause.) Men who dislike the filching of commons whether for quarries or what else. Men who are in favour of fair assessments, and against the scandalously low assessments of noble- men's and gentlemen's country mansions. (Applause.) Of such then is our friend Mr. Occleston and therefore _ . . . _

I hope that North Runcorn will elect him; on Saturday. Believe me, my dear Norman, yours faithfully, Joirar 13nuarNER."—He (the Chairman) could say "Amen " to that letter of Mr. Brunner's, and if they did their duty, Mr. Oecleston would be triumphantly returned at the head of the poll. (Applause.) Mr. J. F. L. Brunner congratulated Runcorn on hav- ing got Mr. Ockleston to stand, for the County Council was not only important for what it would had to do at present, but for what it would have to do in the future, the tendency of legislation being to increase the power of the Council. It was for that reason imp, rtant that they should have Liberals on the Council, a, thov wanted the party not only to make laws, but to itilalinister them. (Applause.) Dr. Hodgson said lie had read Mr. Ockleston's address, Loa fully concurred in it. He thought that he would make a much better representative for a working class constituency than Major Hazlehurst. It was said that they should judge a man by his actions, and if a man was more conspicuous by his absence than his presence, it went to show that his sympathies were not in touch with the constituency. He found that Major Hazlehurst had tiresented some statistics before his audiences, which he said might be relied upon because he had got them from the County Auditor. He commended Major Hazlehurst for his prudence because he could not know the finances of the county himself, inasmuch as though he was a member of the Finance Committee he very rarely honoured them by his presence on that Committee. (Laughter.) So he therefore got A. BRIEF FROM THE COUNTY ACCOUNTANT

and said to the people " Gentlemen here is the county accountant's statement. These are my sentiments. Amen. I hope you will elect me." (Laughter and applause.) Major Hazlehurst had said he had never voted politically on the Council, but he (Mr. Hodgson) pointed out that when the aldermen were elected and it came to a vote as to who should go out in threu years and who in six years, then came the test of THE INDEPENDENCY OF TIIE INDEPENDENT GENTLEMEN. (Applause.) Major Hazlehurst voted so that the gentle- men who should be in for six years were all Tories ex- cept one. Was not that a political vote ? (Hear, hear.) Mr. Ockleston then delivered an address touching upon the various public matters mentioned in his address. _ .
Mr. E. Wynne Fluinphreys then moved a resolution to support Mr. Ockleston. He said he had not intended to take part in the contest,but when he found that men who professed to be on their side were

- STARRING THEM IN THE DARK, he felt, as a Liberal, it was his duty to put private feel- ings on one side, and to come and throw himself into the contest with sueh energy and ability as he might Command. (Applause.) Mr. T. CLEGG seconded the motion, and said he was proud to do so. He had heard a great deal about Inde- pendent candidates. There was no such thing. Major Hazlehurst was a Conservative, and he would vote Con- servative. (Applause.) He had proved it. (Hear,hear.) He also objected to Major Hazlehurst because he had not attended properly to his work, and what was the excuse that lie made ? The syndicate had kept him away from the Council. ("You are right.") What was a syndi- cate? According to their ideas in Runcorn, a syndicate was an institution to buy up old and effete works at fancy prices, and make gentlemen of the owners. (Ap- plause.) Secondly, it was an institution to run down the wages of workmen in order to pay abetter dividend. (Applause.) It was true what he was saying. He had seen the distress in Widnes-75 men turned off this week, 75 off another, and wages reduced. He felt satisfied that a considerable proportion of the works would be closed eventually. Some of them were closed already and all the workmen dismissed without help. And they could not go until it was a syndicate; it was hard lines. Oh No! It was a thing without a heart, without conscience, (laughter and applause)— nothing to appeal to. Well the syndicate had kept Major Hazlehurst busy for three years, although it had not begun then and ended long ago. It was a paltry excuse. If Major Hazlehurst had an employee who at the end of three years said "I have shirked my work, been busy with hunting and shooting, but next three years I will do better." He would give him three years— he would give him three kicks across the street, (laughter). The motion was carried unanimously, and a vote of thanks having been accorded, the Chairman and Mr. Hodgson and Mr. Brunner, the meeting concluded.

div.head: MEETING AT UNION HALL.
div.p: MEETING AT UNION HALL.

I A largely attended meeting in support of Mr. Ockles- ton's candidature was held in Union Hall, Regent-st., on Wednesday night. Mr. A. R. Norman presided, and there were on the platform besides the candidate, Mr. G. Cooke, C.C. of Tattenhall, and Mr. W. R. Earp, C.C., of Preston Broil and other gentlemen. The CHAIRMAN said the Chairman at the meeting in support of Major Hazlf hurst at Mill Brow the other night, in his attempts to be witty

MISHRPRLSRNTED MR. OCHLESTON on the question of Home Rule but he would leave it to Mr. Oalest= to deal with that. His next stroke of sup- posed wit was the statement that it was a ground ot objection on their part that Major Flazlehurst was an ' ornament. They did not object to Major Hazlehurst as lan ornament; their objection was that he was merely an ornament and not a useful and attentive member. (Ap- plause.) They did not object to ornaments if they were useful ornaments. (Laughter and applause.) Mr. G. Corm, C.C., then delivered an address. He said he was sorry to have to appear on a platform to oppose anyone bearing the name of Hazlehurst, who had always been associated in his mind with pleasant recol- lections. But there was a commandment which said— " Honour thy father arid thy mother" : and he had yet to learn that the way to show this honour was by for- , (taking the well-beaten paths ha which they had trod.

(Lpplause.) When men forsook the old paths, and took a fresh course, they made new friends, formed new as- sociations, and they had no right and no title to expect that the old friend would stand by them under those circumstances. (Applause.) Therefore, he felt perfectly at liberty to appear on that platform and

OPPOSE MAJOR RAZLERIIRST. .(Elear, hear.) When a man did not attend to his duties, and did not take an interest in his work, and the party he represented did not see tit to make a change, then it was for the opposite party to take the matter up and try to send another representative to the County Coun- cil. (Applause.) He had always understood that in Runcorn Liberalism was in theascendant,and he trusted the Liberals would show this was w fact by the support they would give Mr. Ocklesten on Satutday. (Ap- plause.) , Mr. W. R. Earp said it was an agreeable task to him to have to address an audience in Runcorn where he knew so many people and where he had so many friends. (Applause.) The statement that 15 Radicals voted against

div.head: VEHICULAR BRIDGE
div.p: THE VEHICULAR BRIDGE

was a very superficial argument. People, whether Radi- cal or Tories, who represented distant parts of Cheshire had no interest at all in Runcorn, and therefore in vot- ing against the spending the money of the county for a bridge, which they said would only benefit Runcorn and Widnes, they were only taking very proper care of the interests of the electors who sent them. To make capital out of a thing like that showed to what ends their opponertts were put to in order to find some excuse or reason for saying something against Mr. Ockleston. If a man lived in Runcorn, if he were the most outrageous Tory possible, and would not vote for the Vehicular Bridge, he should consider such a man

div.head: OUGHT TOBE PUT IN TRE RIVER.
div.p: OUGHT TOBE PUT IN TRE RIVER.

(Laughter and applause.) Dealing with the finance, Mr. Earp said any increase in the county rate ought to have been compensated for by a reduction in the local rates, and pointed out the disadvantage the Council had laboured under in not receiving the usual contributions from the River Weaver Trust. They knew there was such a thing as THE SALT UNION, and thely had driven all the trade away. (Applause.) They had driven away the trade to such an extent that the dues were all required to pay working expenses and interest on the Trust, and consequently there was noth- ing came to the County Council. fhe men at Dutton Workhouse were continually talking about County ex- penditure, and they must know, before they paid the Council demand, what the Council was going to do with it. Some three years ago he could not find a member who could tell him what was the salary of the clerk to the Union, and he never found out until he died, and they advertised for a successor. He would

ADVISE THE GUARDIANS to get to know a little more about what they were doing with their own money before they wanted to know so much about what the Council did with the.money they had to call in. (Laughter and applause.) In conclusion he strongly urged Mr. Ockleston's claims to support, be- cause he came forward with principles and a policy, and said there were certain matters coming before the Coun- cil shortly, such as the River Weaver Trust, control of police, magistrates' clerk's salary, and special duty and allotments, in which the electors of Runcorn would not be properly representated unless they sent Mr. Ockleston to the Council. (Applause.) Mr. Ockleston, who was well received, said he should like to put something straight that was said at a meet- ing of his opponent the other night, by a gentleman, who apparently was like the people of old, who used to spell all the small words and skip all the big ones. (Laughter). It was stated that he was a Home Ruler tor Ireland. It was true. (Laughter and applause). At the same time, he ;Mr. Ockleston) had said he was not a Home Ruler for Ireland on this occasion—he was

A HOME RULER FOR CHESHIRE. (Applause). Cheshire was the word the gentleman could not pronounce. (Laughter aud applause). He believed in the County of Cheshire managing all the affairs of the County through the County Council and the District Councils. And on the first opportunity if he were returned he would vote for the police being placed under the control of the Council, so that they should not act as gamekeepers, but should serve properly the public who paid for them. (Applause). It would also be his object to keep the rates as low as possible be- cause this would be to his advantage and theirs. He (Mr. Ockleston) would support the more equitable rat- ing of gentlemen's mansions and parks, and was strongly of opinion that the Weaver Trust ought to be under the management of the Council, (applause), be- cause he thought it could be managed better than it was at the present time, and he would support a motion having that object in view. (Applause). Pie was also strongly in favour of Technical Education and would do all in his power to continue the grant at present made by the Council. (Applause). The Chairman said it was frequently stated that the Council was merely an administrative body, but while he did not acknowlege this he would admit it for the sake of argument. There was a phrase

ONE LAW FOR Tfill RICII and one law for the poor which had arisen through the law being administered to the advantage of one and the detriment of the other. (Applause.) Now on the County Council they wanted men such as were on the platform that night who would see that thelaws were administered lin favour of the people and nct in favour of the aris- tocracy and those in high places and of those with vested interest. (Applause.) Mr. Boyle moved and Mr. Thomas Cooke seconded a resolution to support Mr. Occleston which was carried unanimously. MAJOR HAZLEHITRST'S ATTENDANCES. Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys said it was apparent from Major Haziehurst's speeches that he did not know how many attendances he had made at the County Council, and in order that he might not remain in ignorance any longer he (Mr. Humphreys) took the liberty of writing to him that morning' enclosing a list, and stating that unless he heard that evening the list was incorrect he should take it that the list as authentic. He had re- ceived no comment upon that list, therefore he would give them one or two particulars. Major Haslehurst's attendances at the meetings of the Council had been better than represented, but he noticed that on their opponent's Committees were several .members of the Board of Commissioners who must know that the real work was not done at the monthly Board meetings but at the Committee meetings. (Applause). With respect to the Council meetings. Major Hazlehurst had missed one in each year. Coming to Committees in the first year he attended five meetings out cf a possible 16; the second year, four out of a possible 23, and in the last year, seven out of erosible 30. Did they wonder that Major Hazlehurst did not know his attendanms when asked? (Laughter and applause). He proposed a 'vote of thanks to the Candidate, to Mr. Earp, and Mr. Cooke for their speeches,and to the Chairman for presid- ing. (Applause). Mr. Withington seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously, and the meeting con- cluded.

div.head: MAJOR HAZLEHLIRST'S CANDIDATURE. MEETING AT MILL BROW.
div.p: MAJOR HAZLEHLIRST'S CANDIDATURE. MEETING AT MILL BROW.

A public meeting in support of the candidature of Major Hazlehurst, for Runcorn North, was held on Saturday night in Mill Brow Board School. There was a good attendance and Mr. J. Meadow- croft was voted to the chair. The Chairman, in opening the proceedings, claimed that Major Hazlehurst's conduct in the past merited their support. Although his attendances had not been SO numerous as some other, members', his opponents had not been able to say that a single vote he had given was wrong, and the Independent party, with which Mr. Hazlehunt identified himself, was no more responsible for the increase in the rate than the Liberal party. Ile understood that the fifteen members of the Council who voted against the proposed Vehicular Bridge were Liberals, and the gentleman who led them was no less a distinguished person than Mr. Hodgson THE IDOL OF THE OPPOSING CANDIDATE.

The ratepayers had to consider whether it was desir- able to increase those fifteen by sending Mr. Ockleaton. (Laughter and applause.) They were quite aware that Mr. Ockleston would vote for the Vehicular Bridge, but the moment he did he became an indepen- ' dent candidate—(applause)..-and followed the foot- steps which Mr. Hazlehurst had followed during the past three years, and which they wished him to follow dur- ing the next three years. (Applause.) MAJOR EIAZLERURST then delivered an address, in which he asserted that his conduct on the Council had been

- ---- ABSOLUTELY INDEPENDENT and had always been guided by common sense and what was best for the ratepayers. He pointed out that the Council was merely an administrative body. The Council had nothing to do with making laws ; all they had to do was to see that those laws were carried out to the bsnefit, of the ratepayers, (Applause.) It was said SIB DID NOT PAY RATES. 1 Directly perhaps he did not, but indirectly he assuredly 11 did—(applause)—and he most positively contradicted the ' statement that he hear.) no interest at all with them iii Runcorn affairs—he had a very great one. (Hear, h 1 As to his at s some time on the last occasion he was ~' 'time before he gave his promise to contest the seat, and he then promised to do his level best forotheratepayers in the time he had at his command Nw .his position was altered. At the present time he was asking them to return him for this reason—that HE WANTED WORK, was willing to work, and he would work if they would give him t he opportunity of doing it. (Applause.) He contradicted the Statement Mr. Cooke that he had only attended made by three occasions during the three the Council on years, and said he was not prepared to gire the absolute he had attended, but he could return of the meetings, tell them THZ STATEMENT WAS ABSOLUTELY PALSE —he did not say with intent .—(Hear, hear.) He be- lieved he had attended 11 out of 12 quarterly meetings, on as possible b' but he would as so e able to give the ex- act nunaber. (Applause.) Tile speaker again dealt with the financial work of the C • ouncil, and in conclusion he pledged himself to do all lie possibly could to further the interests of Ruecor ta iu respect to the vehicular bridge,

technical education, and main roads. (Applause.) He had received complaints of the manner in which the Weights and Measures Act was carried out, and if he could get a statement of the grievances in black and white, he would do his best to get any injustice remedied. (Applause.) Certaillt insinuations had been made about himself on various things' and an extraordinary idea was being attempted to be implanted in the working man with regard to himself about something he could not get to the bottom of. He was perfectly

div.head: PREPARED TO FIGHT STRAIGHT
div.p: PREPARED TO FIGHT STRAIGHT

and never should fight any other way: if he could not be- honest he would not be anything else ; and what ha wanted was that if they were going to hit him, let bins have it straight, and let them see who is th; best. (Ap- plause.) In reply to Mr. J. IL Frith, the candidate said the published report of his interview in the Licensed Vio- tuallers' paper was not what took place. He said he WBg in favour of Sunday Closing,but on business principles he

COULD NOT VOTE -FOR LOCAL OPTION or the direct veto.—Mr. Pope moved the usual resolu- tion of support, and said he had worked for Major Hazlehurst for over ten years, and as he now wanted a place he was pleased to give him a good char- acter (laughter and applause.), and there was no man who had worked for him who would not be very pleased to do the same. (Applause.) Be charged Mr. Temperley with having made use of an inuende against Major Flazlehurst, and he invited him to come forward at the meeting at St. Lukes's, and state plainly what he meant. He advocated conducting these elec- tions on independent lines, and said they could decide what belonged to Runcorn without hearing gentlemen from Crewe, Sandbach, and elsewhere. Let them ask for a little Home Rule on that. (Applause.)—Mr. Han- kinson seconded the motion, and said Major Hazlehurst was not a novice in these public matters.and his speeches had shown that he was well qualified to represent them, irrespective of politics or anything else.—Mr. .J. It. Frith said he had seen nothing in the last three years to cause him to regret having taken part in Major Hazlehurst's election last time. He objected to party politics being introduced into these elections. He had gene in at School Board elections for denominational candidates but be

SkW THE FOOLISHNESS OF IT, and he hoped these local matters would be fought out upon the broad lines of getting the best men possible. (Applause.) It was urged that Major Hazlehurs.t was not a ratepayer, but did the fact that Mr. Ockleston was a ratepayer make him the best man? (Hear, hear.) Did it qualify him to transact the busi- ness of the C.:minty Council better? No. They wanted 1 a man' not a ratepayer ; they wanted those who could dothe best work on the Council. He believed in local option: Major Hazlehurst did not, and he was entitled to his opinion on this question. (Applause.) If it were a question fox' the County Council to decide, he should uot vote for him ; but he thought the matter should not be introduced into it at all.—Mr. H. J. Once also sup- ported the motion and deprecated the introduction of politics.—The motion was carried unanimously and a vote of thanks to the Chairman concluded the proceed- ings.

div.head: MEETING IN THE PUBLIC HALL.
div.p: MEETING IN THE PUBLIC HALL.

A good audience assembled in the Runcorn Public Hall, on Thursday evening, when a public meeting was held in support of the candidate of Major Hazlehurst. Mr. F. J. Norman presided, and he was supported by a large number of local gentlemen. The Chairman, in opening the proceedings, delivered a long address, during which he said there was no re- levancy between a man's political convictions and his capacity for any municipal office, and if they would follow those elections which were fought on a political basis, they would find that men were persecuted as bitterly for their political convictions as men were a. century ago for their religious convictions. (Applause.) The attempt being made to introduce this style in Run- corn was not a new attempt, for on more than two or three occasions, his father during his lifetime had to

PUT HIS HEEL DOWN on this contemptible attempt to drag politics into local , affairs. (Applanse.) If these gentlemen succeeded, it , would not stop at County Council elections ; they would have it connected with Commissioners' elections, then the Board of Guardians; then School Boaid elections would all be fought on these lines. And they would carry it further than that—all their public offices from the law clerk down to the scavengers would be filled on this particular principle. (Applause.) This might suit patriots who had

div.head: MADE POLITICS A TRADE,
div.p: MADE POLITICS A TRADE,

gentlemen who had turned patriotism into a well-paying investment; it would suit busy bodies who could man- age everybody's business but their own. (Applause.) It might suit, a few extreme partisans, but he was proud to think it would not suit the majority of his townsmen. (applause.) He pointed out that he and Major Hazlehurst were diametrically opposed on the temperance question, and at the right time and in the right place he would fight him to the death on that particular point. (Ap- plause.) But it had got nothing to do with this elec- tion, because there was no possibility of the licensing of the Government dealing with the licensing question for many years to come and the matter might be dis- missed. He might tell his temperance friends, that when the licensing question came to be tackled they would find him shoulder to shoulder with them and if they were to obtain what they wanted, they must maintain their independence, and not be tied to the tails of any political party. (Applause.) Mr. Ockles- ton's promise on the direct veto was of as much value as if he promised to play a flute solo at their next penny reading. (Laughter and applause.) Mr. Ockleston was prepared to enter the Council tied to the coat tails of Dr. Hodgson, who so loyally voted against the vehicular bridge. (Applause.) In conclusion the Chairman strongly supported the candidature of Major Hazlehurst, stating that the election was a purely business matter. Major Hazlehurst then delivered an address, and replying to the charge that he was not a ratepayer, said the quantity of rates he paid indirectly quite justified him in coming before them. He did not deny that as to Imperial politics he was a Conservative but so far as local government in the County Council was concerned he had nothing to do with politics at all. (Applause). He had only voted as Common sense dictated and for the benefit of the ratepayers. (Hear hear). As to the ob- jection that he was a magistrate, ho came out un- willingly last year on the solicitation of many who were now working against him, and knowing the difficulties that were before him promised to attend to the duties as well as he could. When he had not attended it was absolutely impossible for him to do so, and he characterised as mean and unfair the statement that he had only attended three meetings. On the previous night at twenty minutes to nine he received a letter from Mr. Humphreys asking him te reply by five o'clock if a list of his attendances en- closed was correct, but it was impossible to reply to it then and so he had to let it slide. That list he found was perfectly correct, but that night he had placed in his hands a printed slip giving his attendances at Com- mittee meetings but omitting the fact that he had at- tended 14 out of 17 Council meetings and that on two occasions when he was absent he was at camp. (Ap-, plause.) He was asked was there no honesty in this concern. But not only were the true facts suppressed but the geqtleman who had stated that he had only made three attendances had not bad the common decency to retract what he had said in public. (Applause.) The speaker then referred to Mr. Barp, who in coming to support Mr. Ockleston, was sailing under false colours as an independent member. (Applause.) It was said that working-men were not favourable to his course, and all sorts of things were said behind his back that he had no chance to repudiate and he asked his opponents to hit him straight, let him stand or fall. (Applause.) But that he was not supported by working-men was absolutely false, and he bad received a latter on the question from a " Liberal well wisher" (which was read) with which he was much gratified. In conclusion he pointed out how much better their local interest could be served by an independent man than by a strong partisan. (Applause.)—Mr. E. Itnison in moving a vote of support to Major Hazlehurst said Mr. Ockleston at each of his meetings had made the statement that Major Hazlehurst was not A ratepayer. He found that during the last ten years up to September, Major Hazlehurst had personally paid in poor' rates the sum of £B6O. (Applause ) Now during that time his opponents' firm, that was, himself and his relatives had only paid £179. (Applause.) And if Mr. Ockleston were to keen paying on at the same rate for the next forty years he would have about paid the same sum as Major Hazlehurst if he never paid another rate. (Applause.) Major Hazlehurst was beneficially inter- ested in property in Runcorn, of the gross annual value of £9Bl. The amount standing to the credit of his opponent was £l4. (Laughter and applause.) And Major Hazlehurst was the man who had no inte- rest whether the rates were low or high. (Applause.) Mr. Imison then gave a trenchant criticism on the speeches that had been delivered by the opposite party, and mentioned as one object the county councillors for the district could seek to attain was the reduction of the fares on the footbridge across the Mersey. (Applause.)— J. R. Frith seconded the motion, stating that his Liberalism was undoubted, but he believed party politics should not be introduced in these contests.—Dr. McDougall supported, urging the claims of the candi- date, because of his local associations, his character,and his ability, and said Mr. Ockleston would only be a puppet in Dr. Hodgson's hands, whose interests were opposed to the vehicular bridge across the Mersey. (Applause.)—Mr. S. Pope and Mr. S. Taylor a'so sup. ported the motion, which was unanimously carried.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
A BIRD-LIMING YOTING THIEF.

At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, Thomas Maley, an extremely diminutive boy, was charged with stealing at Earlestown, on the night of the 26th of Feb., two purses, value is., the property of Wm. Atherton, general dealer. The prosecutor said he lived at Wigan, and had a stall in Earlestown Market. He saw several lads hanging about his stall, but could not be sure that the prisoner was among them. Witness produced the two purses, which had been recovered from the pri- soner, and showed that there was bird-lime on them. P.C. Cameron deposed that about a quarter-past eight on the night in question, he saw the prisoner and some other boys dodging about the stall. He asked Min whether he had taken anything from the stall, and he aid he had not, but two purses and also a stick with bird-lime on the end of it were found upon him. He said he only took one of them. The boy now pleaded guilty, and was sentenced to receive six strokes of the birch rod.

div.head: CHARGES OF THEFT __AGAINST MUSIC HALL SINGERS.
div.p: CHARGES OF THEFT __AGAINST MUSIC HALL SINGERS.

At the Borough Police Court, on Thursday mcrning, Charles Tuckwell, Wm. Munroe, Frederick Varley, and James Fritz, were charged with stealing the previous night from the shop of Messrs. Mawson and Co., 33, Sankey-street, a mackintosh from the shop of Messrs. Unsworth, A, Lyme-street, a cardigan jacket, and from that of Charles McCollum, Market Place, a lady's cloak. The Chief Constable said that the prisoners styled them- selves singers and dancers at music halls, and when not employed there were in the habit of . going about per- forming at public-houses. They had been observed at the White Bull public-house, Market-street, by the bar- man with bundles and acting suspiciously, and infor- mation was given to the police, and Inspector Bowen, Detective-Sergt. Monaghan. and P.C. Dean went to Mrs. Laws's Bank-st., where the prisoners lodged, and found some of the stolen articles, and others belonging to five or six other persons. The prisoners were remanded till to-day.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
FOOTBALL -RUGBY.

The Warrington y. Wigan fixtures always draw a big crowd, and the " gate " of Saturday was no exception to the rule. These meetings of hot rivals are unfortunately often not the most interesting games for spectators to look at, and again that of Saturday was not much of an exception to the rule. The game was too much of a forward nature, and there was too little of the " scienti- fic " element, in the shape of smart passing and running, to be as much worth looking at as it might have been. It, at all events, demonstrated one thing, and that was that the Warrington and Wigan clubs are about as evenly balanced as ever, though on this occasion Warrington just managed to turn the corner in their own favour by one try.

The appearance of the old Edwardians at Runcorn is always welcomed. They were outplayed by the Ches- hire cracks, and were beaten pointless. Widnes had the mortification of going down at home before the deter- mined onslaught of Tyldesley, who won in the last five minutes. St. Helens had to rest satisfied with a draw against Rochdale St. Clements, but the Rees," met with better luck in their engagement with Crompton, the latter being half a-dozen points behind at the finish.

The visit of Bradford to Blackheath was looked upon as a trial of strength between North and South. Black- heath had whipped up a powerful team, and sent the Yorkshiremen home easily beaten, a goal and two tries to nothing being recorded against them. The victorious career of Brighouse Rangers received& check, as they fell before Leeds at Headingley. The Yorkshire Cup is generally expected to be captured by ono of the two clubs just named, unless Bradford regain their lost form.

Not much fault has been found with the composition of the English team selected to oppose Scotland at F,din burgh. The match is expected to rest largely with the forwards, and if the Englishmen only play up to their capabilities they should repeat their triumph of two years ago. ASSOCIATION.

The two semi-finals for the Football Association Cup served to establish another record. The gate money taken at the Braman Lane ground, Sheffield, amounted to upwards of £BOO, this being the largest sum ever received at a semi-final. The receipts account for the presence of upwards of 25,000 spectators, and over 20,000 were gathered together at the other tie at Wol- verhampton. Figures like these go to prove that inter- est in the destiny of the cup is as keen as ever. The prophets were upset once more. For some weeks Sun- derland have been regarded as the certain winners of the Football Association Cups, their football being irre- proachable. But there is evidently no scuh thing as certainty: where football is concerned. They met their masters in Aston Villa, and were effectively knocked out by four goals to one.

For some time after the teams had got to work the Villa had apparently no chance whatever against the skilful northerners. They were almost continually driven on the defence, the combination of the Sunderland men being remarkably fine. They scored early, and it was not until close on the interval that the liirmingham team equalised. The second half saw a marvellous change. The attack was mainly carried on by the Villa, who soon took the lead, and from that point all was over. The tactics of the Sunderland forwards were of a very poor stamp, and they were rarely dangerous. Their complete downfall caused much astonishment. It will be remem- bered that they were beaten on the same ground in the semi-final last year, when Notts County upset them by two goals to none after a drawn game. From this it would appear that Sunderland are not to be seriously feared Oil neutral territory. The success of Aston Villa was as deserved as it was popular. When apparently out of the hunt they pulled themselves together and scored the greatest success of the season!

West Bromwich Albion have proved once more how keenly they throw themselves into cup competitions. They have not nearly so good a record as Notts Forest, and yet experience taNht everybody that they would make a great struggle to gain an entrance into the finalt, Like Sunderland, the Albion went off with irresistible dash. The Forest were out-manceuvred at every point, and at the interval they were in arrear by a goal to nil. After crossing over, however, the Regs showed a vast improvement. Tinsley Lindley equalised and then put on a second point, but this was disallowed, the decision being anything but palatable to the Notts followers. The Forest played well to the end, a draw being the ultimate verdict. The teams will meet again at the same enclo- sure to-day (Saturday). Sheffield would be a better selection for re-playing the tie, as Wolverhampton is so close to West Bromwich that it is not quite fair to the Forest.

Two League games were down for decision, one of which resulted in the defeat of the Rovers and the other in that of Darwen. The Blackburn team were over at Accrington, where they lost bY a goal to none. There was some doubt about the point, against which the Rovers strongly appealed. Notts County were the con- querors of Darwen, victory being represented by three goals to two. WOwen made two sad errors of judg- ment in goal, or Notts would not have won.

There were several surprises in ordinary fixtures. Preston North End made an exhibition of Burnley at Turf Moor, actually beating them by seven goals to two. Everton were also defeated at home, Sheffield United putting on two goals to none. Bootle, too, were unfor- tunate, Crewe Alexandra scoring txfo to one against them.

--- In the Football League competition three matcl.es were decided on Tuesday. At Nottingham Notts County defeated Burnley by five goals to]. ; Sunderland on their own ground beat Bolton Wanderers by 4 goals to 1 ; and at Darwen the home club scored 1 goal against 4 regis- tered by Wolverhampton Wanderers. Everton continued their tour by visiting Grimsby Town, the result of which match was a draw-2 goals each.

div.head: SHOCKING COLLIERY ACCIDET.
div.p: SHOCKING COLLIERY ACCIDET.

Three men named Gerrard, Jones, and Latham were killed on Tuesday at the White Moss Colliery, Skeimers- dale, owing to a collision between two cages inla shaft. A fourth man named John Ratcliffe was so severely injured that he is not expected to live.

div.head: MILLOM MURDER.
div.p: THE MILLOM MURDER.

At Cumberland Assizes, on Thursday, Joseph Wilson, a quarryman, aged twenty-four, was found guilty of the murder of Mrs. Marion Crossmam, with whom he lodged at Millom. On New Year's Day the prisoner Complained about his breakfast, and later shot Mrs. Creasman with a gun. The jury recommended him n to mercy. The Lord Chief Justice sentenced him to death.

THE BRODSWORTH TRAGEDY. MATH OF THE MURDERER. The four Chltdren of the shoemaker Revill, who were murdered by their father on Monday, were buried at Brodsworth, near Doncaster, on Thursday afternoon, the coffins being carried by school childran. Revill died in thp Infirmary in the afternoon from his self-inflicted wound. -

div.head: DISASTER TO A FISHING FLEET.
div.p: THE DISASTER TO A FISHING FLEET.

83 WIDOWS AND 233 ORPHANS. OPORTO, THIIRSDAY,—The total loss of life resulting from the recent disastrous hurricane which overwhelm- ed the fishing fleet has not vet been definitely ascertdined. It is. however, known that 83 of the victims leave widows, and that 233 children have been rendered orphans.
THE ALLEGED BLACKMAILING CASE.

Michael Francis Morland, aged sixty-five, described as a tutor, of 23, St. John-st., Oxford,was again charged at Bow-st., Police Court, on Tuesday,with endeavouring to obtain £7O from Lord Hothfield by false pretences. Earl Russell gaveevidence as to receivine• a letter almost identical in terms with that received by Lord Hothfield, and being; afterwards threatened with legal proceedings by the prisoner if he did not pay £lOO, which the pri- soner said he owed. The prisoner, who reserved his de- fence, was committed for trial.

WARRINIITON Av. Wroax A.—At Wigan. Warrington started against the wind, and the game at once settled down to inside the home, 25. A rush by the Wigan forwards made matters more even, and a clever bit of play by Taylor directly afterwards took the leather in close proximity to the visitors' line. The danger was averted, until a kick being mulled, Aelanrst Erato save a rush. Then Daniels and Lally relieved again, but Warrington, who were having none the best of it, were pressed back. This time Antrobus was the means of clearing, and on his side getting a foothold within home territory, some good work was shown by Hampson, Barnes, Glover, and Bailey. After a bout exchange, kicking Daniels threw across to Westall„ who failed to round his man, play locating close to the Wigan line. A bad pass lost all the advantage gained, the visitors' lines being once more assailed. Some protracted monotonous scrimmages ensued, and on the ball becoming loose Taylor secured possession, and eluding the efforts to stop him gained a fine try, which was converted. Following the kick off, Potts made a grand run, this being supple- mented by Hampson, Higharn, and Bailey making a fine. dribble to the line. ..T. Warburton and Lally affected a capital dribble, only to see the leather returned into the visitors' territory. Here followed a splendid bit of work by Bailey and Antrobus ; but at half the score was— Wigan 1 goal to nil. Resuming hostilities,. Rawson-, Higham, Barnes, and Molyneaux were notable in their endeavours to break away, but Rawlison kicked to mid- field. The ball was returned,. Barnes, by a firm effort,. stopping Sinclair before he could reply, and the ball being dribbled over, Hampson scored, the place failing. The game for some time after this settled down into monotonous scrimmages, until Hampson, putting in a high pant, the ball was rushed by Glover, Forster, and Molyneaux to the goal posts. A quick passing movement by the Warrington backs was responded to by a long kick by Rawlinson. Ashurst replied, and again the ball was quickly taken to the line, a grand drop by Potts sailing just outside the posts. The drop out was of little avail to the home team, who were now having all the worst of the game, some splendid play by Hampson being witnessed, and the ball was again dribbled over, but nothing beyond a minor accrued. After this from a quick throw out, Hampson passed finely to Daniels, who kicked and followed up, causing play to locate in the home quarters, and despite all attempts to score, Wigan kept their lines intact, and retired winners by 1-goalto • 0-1-3.

div.head: WARRINGTON v. WIGAN:
div.p: WARRINGTON v. WIGAN:

The meeting of Warrington and Wigan stood out as the mast prominent entagement in the County Palatine on Saturday, and as a consequence, a large " gate" was recorded. The match was the return engagement, and the one at Wigan having ended in a favourable draw in a favourable draw in favour of our local team, Warrington enthusiasts were jubilant at the fact that there was a probability at last of their favourities cheok- ing the phenomenal series of successes achieved by Wigan during the last three seasons. The weather pro- mised anything but an encouraging aspect for a large "gate "during the early hours of the morning, but as the day wore on the sun came out in all its brilliancy and the match was fought under conditions agreeable both for player and spectator. There would be fully 8,000 spectators present when the game was commenced, and Warrington having won the toss preferred to defend the railway goal. Atkinson kicked off, and Evans and Seddon exchang- ing ticks, the first scrimmage was fought at centre. Halliwell and Mitchinson showed up with passing from the pack, but the sure tackling of Heesoin and Webster did not allow of much progress. Seddon was soon floored, and then the Warrington forwards broke away, and a permanent position was taken up near the Wighn quarter flag. Heesom cleverly made his mark, which Turner failed to utilise, and although Singleton slightly relieved, the two Bates passed well, James winding up the sequence by regaining the lost ground. The same player next initiated a passing movement, and when opposition had been partially cleared, the chance was knocked on. Webster was busy in preventing Wallwork, who had a host of opportunities of displaying his speed, and Turner, Buckley, Donohue, and Teare, from one rush, were almost over. Boscow was called upon to check an advance, and, needless to say, he was not found wanting. However, the Wiganers, by the aid of Atkinson and McNamara, reached the half-way flag, but Warrington, headed by Berry and Donohue,. soon had the oval Nick on the Wigan lines. For obstruction ' the visitors lost ground, and a sharp passing bout saw Evans being well tackled by Atkinson. The last-named came through a scrimmage in fine style, Heesom saving admirably. James Bate dribbled well, and J. Halliwell and Mitchinson both tested Boscow with a like result, that Wigan hoid to act on the defensive. Eventu- ally the oval was found careering near the Wigan line, and some sharp rushing bus i nes wails witnessed. From some loose play, the oval fell into the hands of Handles, and this player, showing excellent judgment, passed to Webster when the course was clear, and the winning point of the day was scored. Cheer after cheer bailed Warrington's suc- cess, Evans failing at a difficult place. The restart saw Evans making his mark, and Ashton following up well spoiled the return. Webster failed to field, the oval from a low pass by John Bate, and although Boscow was called upon in Close quarters, he cleverly screwed into touch near the quarter flag. So far, Wigan had had all the 'worst of the play, whilst J. Halliwell was compelled to save his charge. Neutral gronnd saw operations on the drop-out, and Evans and Boscow kicking judiciously their efforts were aided by an admirable rush, in which Turner, Knowles, and Buckley were the leaders. The Bates and Teare passed neatly, hut without effect,whilst a grand kick by J. Halliwell was applauded to the echo. Eventually Unsworth got clear, but Atkinson passed into Webster's hands, and once more Wigan defended. James Bate tricked his opponentefinely, but Atkinson, making amends for his mistake a moment ago, dribbled finely up the field. and lodged the .game for the first time at Warrington quarters. Buckley was the means of changing the venue, whilst a grand piece of work by Evans, in passing across to Heesom, saw the latter's passto Webster being charged. The game was taken direct to the home 'lines, but Seddon's slowness saw Evans clearing finely, and sperations being taken to half-way.' The interval was signalled with the score-- Warrington one try ; Wigan, nil. With two points of a lead the game was resumed, and for the first five minutes exchange kicking monopolised the attention. Turner deposited in touch at half-way, and from h line-out Thorniley and Teare got away, and matters again assumed a serious aspect for Wigan. An invasion of Warrington ground was forthcoming, and Sed don was particularly fortunate in getting in a kick when pressed. Heesom saved his lines splendidly, whilst a series of hot scrimmages rendered the game monotonous. Wigan apparently had the goal at their mercy on one occasion, but James Bate snapping up the oval from their feet,ran and punted out cif danger. The visiting. backs again passed well, Wallwork-having a futile shot at goal. John Bate,with tricky tatics,presscd the game near half-way, whilst Webster appeared in a new depar- ture in saving a rush. Forward play, at which Wigan were masters, marked a lengthened period of this half. The monotonous display was eventually relieved, for the Bates got the oval working on the popular side, and exchanging fully half a dozen times, Evans was collared when within easy reach of the line, A minor was con- ceded a moment later. Evans met the restart, and Halliwell kibking well and Seddon dodging finely,. Wigan once more pressed. The Bates and Thornily passed well, whilst Knowles made his mark in a favourabl" position, but Turner's attempt at goal was charged. The visitors made strenuous efforts near the close: but the defence of Boscow, Evans, and Heesom, could not b,e overcome, and in theend Warrington retired victors by a try end two minors to a minor. Teams :—Warrington : Boscow, back ; Webster. Heesom. and Evans, three-quarter backs ; John T. Bate and James Bate, half-backs • Ashton, Fair. Turner, Bandies, Berry. Denohue, Buckley, Thornily, Knowles, and Teare, forwards. Wigan : J. Halliwell, back ; Wallwork, Seddon, and Singleton, three-quarter backs ; Mitchinson and W. Barnwell, half backs ; Rigby,Atkin- son, Wardle, Unsworth, Lance, M'Namara,. Grundy, Fredericks, and R. Seddon, forwards. ASSOCIATION. WARRINGTON v. SOUTH WEST MANCHESTER.

The return match between these two clubs was played on Saturday, on the ground of the latter club. The first fixture resulted in a win for Warrington by three goals to two. The visitors' team was somewhat disorganised, three forwards being absent. They went with ten men, and a substitute was picked up on the field. Before the play commenced each team went under the operation of being photographed. Warrington, 'winning the• toss, elected to play up hill and with the wind. The home • team started the game, but the visiting forwards ob-' tamed pmssession and invaded the home quarters but were repelled by the backs. Tickle and Powell ran down the left, the latter shooting at goal, but the goalkeeper easily save,. play continued in the home half, shots being sent in by T. Mather, Powell, and Pierpoint, but all were eventually cleared. A succession of goal kicks now followed, owing to the visiting team pressing their opponents strongly. The home forwards took up the running, but were cleared out by a huge kick from the visiting centre-half. Warrington now forced a corner,but nothing came of it. The home right pair now went down the field, and matters looked dan- gerous for the visitors, but Jones ran out and sent the ball well down the field. Shortly afterwards a foul was awarded the visitors, and from the free kick, which was splendidly placed by the centre half, the ball hovered about the home goal, till finally it was shot through by Pierpoint, thus drawing firstblood for Warrington, From the restart, the visitors were soon in the home quarters, the half-backs and eacks feeding the forwardsnieely and easily repelling the incursions of the home forwards, whose efforts were generally individual, and as a conse- quence were easily disposed of by the visiting backs,

div.head: NER,
