. who both played- ont of their best games. Several corners now fell to the Warrington men but nothing tangible accrued. Half-time was now called, the score reading Warrington 1, S. W. Manchester On the resumption of play, the home foevrards took up the running, but their final efforts were decidedly weak, the ball travelling harmlessty over the line. The visitors now had a look in, and gained a* corner, with thesame result. Later on, when bn a good position for shooting T. Mather was given offside. A foul close in the visit- ing goal was got rid of at the expense of a corner. Again the visitors went for their opponenta' goal, and, aided by some good judiciou,s kicking on the part of the backs,the forwards forced another corner, but could not turn it to a practical account. The home forward*, now carne with a rush, and from a pass from the right i wing the Inside left scored a very doubtful goal, he be— ing clearly offside. The point was appealed against,. but the referee allowed it, this making the- teams equal in point of scoring. Some scrambling play now en- sued, each side pressing in turn.. Time was now called, leaving the match drawn. The visiting team had de- cldedly the best of matters throughout, and,considering the weakened state of the forwards, did very well. The goalkeeper and backs played splendidly, with the excel>, tion of the left half, whose kicking at times, was very poor. Forward, Tickle, T. Mather, Powell, and Pier 4 point, did well, the last-named having to play with the substitute (who, it would only be fair to state, played a good game), and also was on his wrong wing. Pierpoint is one of the Reserve forwards, but judging from his play on Saturday last, he merits a further trial in the first team. The match was pleasantly contested throughout, and no doubt fixtures will be arranged for =other season.

div.head: AMUSING SCENE AT ST. HELENS POLICE COURT.
div.p: AMUSING SCENE AT ST. HELENS POLICE COURT.

An amusing incident occurred in the police court' on Monday, when the magistrates present were Mr. W. 1., Pilkington and Alderman C. J. Bishop. A+ respectably-dressed woman was charged under the name of "Daisy Pownall " with being drunk and, disorderly in Eccleston-st. When the name was called the prisoner emphatically declared that that was not her name, and to the intense amusement ef every one in court said her real name was Marguerite Violet Maude Purnell.—The Clerk: Were you drunk ? Prisoner r Certainly not, sir.—When the officer had con- • eluded his evidence, prisoner exclaimed—Do you know God's commandments? Do you know that a false swearer never enters the kingdom of heaven ?? (Laughter.) She concluded with the assertion that the constable had been put there for wilful and cor- rupt perjury. She threatened to "bring him up" for perjury, and advised the Chief Constable, amidst great* laughter,. to send him to Eccleston Churchyard "to meditate among the tombs." She was fined 2s. ed. and. costs, whereupon she asked the magistrates to take it* out of the constable's wages, adding that she had only a crossed cheque that darin her possession. She appealed to be spared the infliction of a removal " downstairs," and.when leaving the court, in company with an officer, , she expressed a hope that the bench would reduce the constable in the ranks who had given evidence against her. During these proceedings those present in court were almost convulsed with laughter.

div.head: WARRINGTON GYMNASIUM.
div.p: WARRINGTON GYMNASIUM.
THE CHALLENGE fIIELD COAPETITION.

On Saturday evening the team of the Warring- , ton Gymnasium met the Exeter Hall (London) team in the Neon I round of the competition for the challenge shield of the National Physical Recreation Society. The contest on this occasion took place at Warrington Gymnasium, and it was witnessed by a crowded audience. Mr. T. Morrid presided. The judge was Mr. R. E. Thomas, of Leeds. The teams, which each consisted of eight members,com- peted in threelexercises—clubs, rings, and the run- ning jump... The performances with clubs were gone through 'in a remarkably graceful manner by both teams, and were much applauded by the audience. The teams were evidently pretty nearly equal, and this was shown by the award of the judge who gave Warrington 140 points and Exeter Hall 135. In the rings competition the teams were also remarkably equal, both of them displaying a proficiency which was clearly the result of careful training. For this exercise Exeter Hall were given IEI3 points and Warrington 102. Up to this point Warrington had slightly the best of the contest, but as soon as jumping began it was seen that the visitors were remarkably strong in this department Three or four a the Warrington athletes were soon out, but only one of the Londoners made what„ in any sense, could be described as a poor display Walsh 'and Podniore and Warren, and especially the first-named, did fairly well for Warrington, but while Walsh's score, which was the highest on the home side, was 13, no fewer than five of the visitors attained or excelled that figure. T. W. Nye, whose record is said to he five feet eight inches, proved himself to be particularly adept in topping the rod, and he was the means of securing 16 marks for his side on the jumping. In the end Exeter Hall were declared the winners by .16 points. It should be added that in the course of the meeting Mr. T. Morris announced that it was intended to hold a bazaar in the autumn towards paying off the debt on the Gymnasium. The following are the scores of the two teams : Total.

div.p: THE STRIKE OF -GAS STOVE MAKERS AT WARRINGTON. MEETING OF THE STRIKERS.

• A meeting of the workmen of Messrs. Richmond and Co., now on strike was held at Bridge Foot, on Sunday morning. Mr. John Price president of the Warrington Trades Council, and secretary of the local navvies and general labourers' union, presided, and on the roney which was used as a platform, he was somported by Mr. W. H. Bullock, secretary of the Tranes Comacil, Mr. A. E, Benjamin, delegate to the Trades' Council, Mr. 7 B. Malkin, secretary of the Warrington Ironworkers' Union, Mr. 11. Sanders general secretary to the gas stove grate werkers' ;union, Mr. John Willetts, secretary to the Warring- ton branch of that union, Mr. Wright, vice-president 'of the Warrington filesmiths' union, and Mr. J. Rudge. There 'mos a large attendance.

The CHAIRMAN% said the men on, strike were out of employment because they dared to act according to the dictates of their conscience. They were not there that morning to fall out with the employers or to cause any disturbance, but to•encourage the men by showing that they sympathised with them in their struggle.,, and in- ' tended to give theintail the moral support they conk). They-believed that as workmen of Warrington they had not been fairly treated, and they were there to demand that they should be better treated in the future. He was glad to find that every one of the men had stood firm to his principles during the week, and had not shown the white feather, that everyone had done his best to uphold the principles of trades unionism and the dignity of labour. Mr. SANDERS then addressed the meeting. He said the matter in dispute between Messrs. Richmond and their men was the fact of the men having joined the union. The masters had become terrified. When the question of prices came upamongst the fitters of the farm the union men said they could not accept those offered. A deputation met the directors, who conceded what would havo been accepted as satisfactory in point of payment, but concluded by saying "You must go to your work as non-union, men.' He asked was it fair, honourable,. Englishman-like for a man to sell his principles, at the price of a few 'pence, to his employers? No, and the- day had gone by whea the workers would be content to act upon the ukase of Messrs. Richmond and Co., or any other employers in the country. The object of the union was simply to maintain a fair and equitable arrangement , between employer-and workman: all they asked for was a fair pay for a fair day's work. 99 out or every MOP , union men if told that they must leave the unioni or their employ, as in the case of Messrs. Richmond,. Would answer that they would leave their employ. 'And why? Because he knew those men were best paid and best protected -where trades unions, existed, and wherever you found disorganisation, you found tyranny and injustice. The crux-of the whole qisestion now in dispute was unionism or non-unionism. After explain- ing the negotiations between the union and the Directors. , of the firm as already reported, he stated that Mr Wilsey one of the Directors said they bad- no objec- tion to unionists as a body, but they Wit° the national union of stove. grate workers. Messrs-. Richmond and Co. had entered upon the struggle,-.but he should certainly say they had not fairly estimated what it meant; they could not have calculated the forces, they had to contend with.' (Applause.) if they thought r they-were only fighting one union they made a great Mistake. Mr. Sanders advised the strikers-to use no un- due influence or violence with the," knobsticks," and charged the police with having been over realous in the intereets of the employers and overstepped the bounds- of the law, declaring that they had no right to. interfere with the strikers 40 'long as they did not resort to vio- lence: ) One of the strikers had been broughtbefore the magistrates on a, charge of intimidationi, and a local legal celebrity in cross-examination of one. of the wit- nesses asked him, if he did not knew, he was liable to three months' iniprisonment for picketing.. The speaker characterised this as a new version ofi the law and a blundering statement, and hoped the- trades unionists. would not be misled by it. Mr. Struocxmoven the following resolution :—"That this meeting desires to express its deep.sympathy with our fellow Trades Unionists who have-been called upon by their employers, Messrs. ' Richmond 'and CO.. of War- rington, either to leave -the ranks of Trades' Unionism., or leave their employ. We commend the, workmen for the course which they have taken, and pledge ourselves to render them every possible financial, and moral sup port as long as the struggle lasts." Mr. Wrmarrrs-secooded. He remarked that it was not so much the employers as the "'scabs "' they had to fight, whom he described as unworthy the name of men and as reptiles, Mr. WRIGHT expressed the opinion that the police of Warrington, as having great grievances of their own, ought to have some feeling of- sympathy with the strikers.

The motion was carried with practical, unanimity. Mr. BENJAMIN proposed the following resolution "That this meeting further desires to protest against any undue influence on the part of the police, and con- demns the action of the borough magistrates on Fridaylast in convicting a striker of intimidation whom they acquitted of assault" He remarked that referring to the " Examiner " of last week he found it pretty clearly laid down by the Town Clerk,.whom he took to he the most prominent lawyer of the town, that the strikers had a right to combine, .to picket, and to apeak to the non- unionists filling their places, but not ta use any undue influence or violencetowards them, This, he believed, had since been confirmed by the Town Clerk. The magistrates ought if they convicted the man before them of anything, to have convicted him, of assault and dis- missed him on the charge of intimidation. The chair- man of the Bench, said they must fine -the defendant pretty heavily becausb the fine would be subscribed by his fellow-workmen, ("Shame"), That showed he had no sympathy with the working,men. Mr. MeLuNseconded the motion: Be observed in the course of a brief speech, that it had been stated before the labour commission, that where there was the most trades' unionism there were the best paying shops for the employers. 'Mr. }LEDGE supported the motion, which was carried. Mr. SANDERS rose to propose a vote of thanks to the chairman, but caused considerable excitement by ex- claiming" What do you think ?? The man who has more than anyone caused the strike has the Cheek and ,impudence tabe present at this meeting" and pointed out Mr. Ward,, manager for Messrs. Richmond and Cu;, desiring the crowd to have good look at him, and challenging him to como forward and defend himself. Mr. WARDi amidst loud expressions of antagonism, ascended the rolley.. He nide, lot of the statements made that morning werefigse. ("They are not.") The men that had worked for Messrs. Richmond made more

money than the men under any other firm in the trade. (" Question, "and " Not true.") The reason of the strike was that two men came to him asking for a job so that they might learn the particular class of work. Experienced men would have made 38s. to 425. a week, but these men only made 145.. and 24.5. Here Mr. Ward was interrupted by considerable noise. Mr. SANDERS appealed for order, saying : "I am in charge of this strike, and if 'cannot do Mr. Ward down I will sulTer to be done down." The disturbance con- tinuing, Police Inspector BOWEN came forward and said if the meeting could not continue peaceably, he should have to bring a force of police to disperse it. The CHAIRMAN appealed for order, and silence ensued. Mr. WARD continued his remarks. He said the two men had afterwards informed him that the union would not allow them to work for the wages named. He swore at them, and told them they must take it or leave. That WES why the unionists went out. Mr. Buttocs asked him why the firm objected to the stove grate workers' union? Mr. Ws.firo : I am not at liberty to say anything farther. (Loud laughter.) Mr. SANDERS replied, denying the truth of the state- ments and referring to the statement of the firm in the press in confirmation of his denial. He admitted that the firm paid their moulders well, but said they paid their fitters poor prices. If the firm would recog- nise the union the men were ready to go back, but they . .

vnuld not go back as non-union men. (Loud applause.) Mr. WARD attempted to speak again, but the Chair- man closed the meeting, challenging him, however, to a dlscugsiouthere to-morrow (Sunday) morning. £2 7s. was collected on the spot in aid of the strikers.

Her Majesty's steamer Ramillies, the largest warship in the world, was on Tuesday launched at Glasgow, the christening ceremony being performed by the Duchess of Abercorn. Mr. T. Gair Ashton has been adopted by the Hyde Liberals as their candidate at the next election A Dublin contemporary states that Avondale thehouse and estate of the late Mr. Parnell, are about to be sold, Mr. John Parnell having resolved to return to America. Mr. Maden, M.P., attended a meeting at Haslingden on Saturday. He said he believed the general election would take place between Easter and Whitsuntide.

The claims already lodged with the Berlin, authorities in connection with last week's labour riots have reached 30,000 marks, and are expected to reach, 50,000 marks in all. The authorities are devising means to find work for the unemployed. All arrangements are now completegl for the departure of the Queen for the Continent on the 17,th inst. The Worcestershire and Staffordshire spike-nail makers have resolved to strike on Saturday, failing an advance of 15 per cent. in wages. On Wednesday night, Capt. Tariman. of Kingston-on- Thames, was found dead near Grove Ferry Station. Death is attributed to the accidental exploding of a gun which the deceased was carrying..

A Kirkcaldy correspondent telegraphs that th,o, politi- cal situation remains unchanged. Despite Mr. Glad- stone's suggestion, Lord Ifitzmaurice and Mr. Lewis express their determination to fight to the ec,d. The alleged "strong man" San?son was again brought up in London, on Thursday, on the charge of stealing jewellers from a married woman named Bernstein, who is "connected witn, the stage." The, prosecutrix made some very compromising aramissiow, am, the o,so was again adionrned.

The Bill of the Manchester Ship•Carrad Company pro- viding that, notwithstanding anything contained in the provisions of their Act of 1885; the company may apply to the Board of Trade at any time to inepect their- de- viation railways, and the Board may approve of the opening of such railways, eame before the examiners, of the standing orders of the Illouse of Lords, on Tuesday, when it was proved that theronseat of the shareholders at the Wharncliffe meeting had been given to the Bill, and it passed this stage without opposition. VISIT OF THE SHAREHOLDERS COMMITTEE!, The committee of the recently forrnedo Ship Canal! Shareholders' Association inspected the Ship Canal Works, from Manchester to Eastham Locks on Saturday. The party (about 25) started from Pomona in a special train. under the guidance of Mr. Leader Williams, chief engineer of the company, and their number included Mr, Alderman Forrest (chairman of the association),. Mr, Reuben Spencer, Mr. Hilton Greaves, Mr. J. Greaves. Dr. W. Armstrong then. secretary). The day was fine, , and, therefore, admirably adapted for an inspection of the works. The party left Manchester shortly after half-past ten o'clock in the forenoon, an inspectiembeing made of the Salford Docks, the Barton locks and swing bridge, and the locks and "skew" bridge at Latchford. On arriving at Stockton Heath, at one o'cleck an adjournment was made to the Saracen's • Head Hotel, whore the party sat down to an excellent dinner which had been provided by the proprie- tor, Mr. T. 0. Speakman, and to which ample justice was done. Dinner over, Alderman Forrest said as rnerabers of the association they were now gathering information which ought to have been obtained months ago, namely, a correct idea of the engineering and land difficulties, and of the impulses of the forces of nature.' Now that more light had been thrown on the progress of the Works, the light of public opinion, he felt sure' that that opinion would never be withdrawn until they saw ships floating from Easttiam to Manchester. Hecone eluded by proposing "Prosperity to the Ship Canal Cb,,. coupled with the name of Mr. Leader Willigma.(Applaumr,)/1 Mr. Leader Williams responded to the toast, and said he thanked the Chairman most heartily fer the kind 'way in which he had spoken. In the early stage of the' undertaking he paid for 6)0 ordidary shares—he paid them up in full—arid he had never sold a share, therefore, he thought that that would show that he was not only interested in .the scheme, but believed 'int it. Mr. Spencer said they all regretted Mr. Walker's death, as he was a man of great ability, and very capable as a contractor and financier. e felt that day, more than he had ever felt before, that he would never rest satisfied until he saw the water flaw- log into the docks and the great undertaking completed. --Cbuncillor Mandley, of Salford, said their feelings were! I little premature, as the,y had not yet seen the most !difficult operations which were being carried out on the! Canal—operations which exercised the thought and care. of the engineers. He had been told that the construc- tion of the wall at Runcorn would cost £1,000'4600.' He should like to see how that work was progressing. The party than proceeded on their journey to Eastham., At !Weston, Mr,. Marshall Stevens met the committee,and at ' Raotham a steamer was in waiting to convey the pasty,to. the Prince's landing stage at Liverpool.

div.head: ORDINARY GENERAL MEETING.
div.p: ORDINARY GENERAL MEETING.

The thirteenth ordinary general meeting of the .share- holders of the Manchester Ship Canal Company, .was held on Monday, at the Concert Hall, Peter-st.,Manches-- ter. • The hall was densely crowded. Lord Egerton of Tatton, chairman of the directors, presided, and in pro- posing the adoption of the report, which was taken as read, reviewed the causes why the canal had not . been opened, as was intended, on the Ist January, 1892.!. The. Chairman concluded a lengthened statementemid ap- plause by saying that the works were, in spite of diffiliul- ties, approaching completion, and it was reasonable to hope that the canal would be open next year.—Mr. LK. ' Bythell, in seconding the motion, said that theshare- holders had no need to be despondent at all. It waste- lieved that the canal would be opened next yealyind they would soon gain a substantial return for their patience. Mr. Alexander Forrest, chairman of the Ship Canal Shareholders' Association, who next, ad- dressed the meeting, said that meeting marked 'a new era in the history of, the Snip Canal. The directors had unburdened themselves. His only regret was that . that wat not done two or three years ago. The resolution waS adopted, and on the motion. of ' Mr. Bythell, seconded by ,Mr. S. R. Platt, Lord Egerton was unanimously re-elected. Sir Edward Jenkiason, Mr. W. J. Crossley, Mr. Charles J. Galloway, the other- retiring 'directors, were also unanimously re-elected: Alderman Bosdin T. Leech, Mayor of Manchesterf.was ' unanimously re-elected the auditor of the company. At ' aspecial meeting subsequently held, the shareholders approved of the Bill now before Parliament for conferr- lag further powers on the company

div.head: SUICIDE AT PADGATE:
div.p: SUICIDE AT PADGATE:

Some"months ago a man named Thomas Worsley, a puddler, residing at 67, ilaydock-et., Warrington, was brought before the magistrates on a chargs-ot attempting self-destruction, by cutting his throat, and the evidence disclosed that a decided suicidal tendency:had existed in the man's mind for some time previous. It was supposed that he had been so far cured of this propensity that hi was-safe-in the Charge of his family, and he was dismissed. 'Unfor- tunately, it. has proved to be too deeply rooted, for the result of his being set at large has been that it has since asserted itself with only too fatal con- sequences. The circumstancm were detailed in an inquest which was held by Mr.. S.. I.kiig- house, coroner, at the Dog and Partridge, POulton.— Mary Worsley, wife of the deceased, stated that she last saw her husband on Monday week. On that day, he said that he was going out for a walk. She, identified the body as that of her husband. The deceased had lately suffered from influenza, and was very lowvspirited. He had been attended by Dr. Adams.--JosepnWorsley, son, said that he last saw his father alive a week ago, They had taken great care of him since his previous attempt at suicide, but his manner was very peculiar,. He identi- fied the knife found on the deceased as his owm.—Williant Bennett, farmer, Poulton, stated that he found the de- ceased in a.shed on his land on the 265 h ult. He at once communicated with the police.--Sergeant Barnes deposed that on the 26'h of February he was called to. a shed on Mr. Rennett's land, on the south side of the. canal. He found the deceased man lying on his back on some hay. His windpipe was cut clean through. He found the knife produced on him, and also 103. ltd. The man's right hand was covered with blood. His clothing was wet as if he had been in the water—The jury returned a verdict that the deceased had committed suicide whilst suffering from temporary insanity.

div.head: PASSING CROWD.
div.p: THE PASSING CROWD.

I The.. Passing Ocardllisn: Crowd" is a phrase coined in the spirit (11 indifference. Yet, to a man, of what Plato universal sympathies, and even to the plain ry, denizens of this world, what can be more . interesting than "the passing crowd ?" Does not this tide .of human beings, which we daily see . •Passing tong the ways of this world, consist of , .persons animated by the same spark of the Divine "setkoe, and partaking of the .same high destinies With Ourselves? Let us stand still but for a moment iv . .."11,e midst of this busy and seemingly careless , 8eQ)(1, and consider what they are or may be whom We I,ee around us. In the hurry of the passing show 4" of our own sensations, we see but a series of "known faces ; but this is no reason why we should regard them with indifference. Many of ' Ilie-se persons, if we knew their histories, would rivet our admiration by the ability, worth, benevo- lence, or piety which they have displayed in their 'various paths through life. Many would excite our Warmest interest by their sufferings—sufferings, Perhaps, borne meekly and well, and more for the 4 ~64,Le of others than themselves. How many tales 't human weal and woe, of glory and of humiliation, ceuld be told by those beings, whom, in passing, we i'egard not ! Unvalued as they are by us, how many taa; good as ourselves repose upon them the affec- ?ens of bounteous hearts, and would not want them or axty earthly compensation! Every one of these Plearsous, in all probability, retains in his bosom the ' ? erished recollections of early happy days, spent, scene which "they ne'er forget, though• there they are forgot," with friends and fellows- fe ho, though now far removed in distance and in rtune are never to be given up by the heart. Ev ' „„erY one of these individuals, in all probability, ,7:r'es still deeper in the recesses' of feeling the -`; .„terribranc.e in that chapter of romance in the life ,'''', every man, an earnest early attachment, oon- wed in the fervour of youth, unstained by the Slightest thought of self, and for a time purifying ..4141 elevating the character far above its ordinary tlandard. Beneath all this gloss of the world— is cold conventional aspect, which all more or present, and which the business of life renders 01e4sary—there resides for certain a fountain goodness pure in its inner depths as the lymph k• tee . , distilled, and ready on every proper occasion ' ll out in the exercise of the noblest duties. 01;4134gh all may seem bat a hunt after worldly at j, ,ee tBo the great majority of these individuals can, ' 4„'oe proper time, cast aside all earthly thoughts, e;',o-;eonamunic,ate directly with the being whom ...4 fathers have taught them to worship, and Will and attributes have, been taught to man puelniediately by Himself. Perhaps many of these 13,,liten8 are of a loftier aspect than ourselves, and ze-v7rgthteoles, essphere removed above our own. But, if the barrier of mere worldly farm taken out of the way, it is possible that we i rila interchange sympathies with these persons as , Pee,_l9 and cordially as with any of our own class. , . keruaPs they are of an inferior order; but timy „e only inferior in certain circumstances, which ;raid never interpose to prevent the flow of feeling r kind. The great common features of bl-roan nature remain; and let is never forget how respect is due to the very impress of humanity ~ "10 type of the divine nature Weir.; Even where fellow-creatures are degraded by vice end rovett . TN Y. let us still be gentle in our judging'. • . .40:4Zr!ens fortunes which We every day see befall- -1,-;14, tht inemberS Of a single family, after they 11" th ,:`rt, oft in their several paths through life, teach , a, at : Zi:_reer of existence is destined. Besides, do not it is not to every one that success in the th: arrangements of society at once necessitate , top subJection of an immense multitude to humble Iv 1, and give rise to 'temptations, before which the teak and uninstructed can scarcely escape falling? even beneath the soiled face of the poor -lizsn, there may be aspirations after some wague excellence, which hard fate has denied him the ,!Teans of attaining, though the very wish to obtain „''' is itself ennobling. The very mendicant was et always so; he, too, has had his undegraded d happier days, upon the recollection of which, "erue remnant of better feeling may still repose. het l'hese, I humbly think, are reasons why we should, Iv look with coldness upon any masses of men 4 ith whom it may be our lot to mingle. It is the ature of a good man to conclude that others are 01:1 himself ; tvh and if we take the crowd promiscu- eeirlYeL;e can never be far wrong in thinking that worthy and well-directed feelings in it as is our own bosoms.

div.head: trtters to the ebttor.
div.p: trtters to the ebttor.
EARLESTOWN WATER SUPPLY.

should much like to ask the Chairman of Com- missioners how it is that Newton has an almost con- tinuous supply of water, and that parts of Earlestown, notably along the road to the Common, have their supply stopped from about 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. every day, tit-is having been the case for some months past. Further: Have the London and North-west Railway Company the power to ride roughshod over some portion of the inhabitants in this arbitrary manner? And, if so, who were the idiots who gave them this power? If the Present Commissioners are responsible, then I have no hesitation in saying that at the next election they should be relegated to that "blissful bourne" where only block- beads—culpable, or otherwise—are herded together, to be kept out of mischief; and if some previous Commis- sioners were guilty of the mad folly, then by all means let us erect a statue made of some durable but ignoble materials, to tell the tale. speak warmly, because feelingly,'on this important =atter. To think that any Company or Corporation can, st will, stop one of the main springs of life, is an enormity not to be tolerated ; and I hope, by ventilating the matter publicly, a stop will be put to a practice that savours more of the long-past ages than the present day. A SUFFERRR. 1,3, '92.

div.head: BRITISH. MEDICAL ASSOCIATION.
div.p: BRITISH. MEDICAL ASSOCIATION.

Sir, —I forward to you subjoined herewith a copy of resolution passed at a meeting of the Committee of the British Medical Association appointed to consider legis- lation for Habitual Inebriates, which was afterwards placed before the Council of the Association and approved and confirmed. I trust you will assist in the work of completing the compulsory legislation on the subject by petitioning Parliament.-1 am, your obedient servant, NORMAN KERR, M.D.,

Ctsairman of the Inebriates' Legislation Committee. 429, Strand, W.C. February. 1892. [COPY.] Resolved : That this Committee is gratified to observe the marked advance in public opinion in favour of legisla. tion or the compulsory reception and detention, in special homes for curative purposes,of such diseased inebriates as have had their will power so broken down as to be unable of their own accord to apply for such admission and de- tention. In view of this change of general opinion this meeting recommends to the Council of the Association that an appeal be issued by this Committee to all associa- tions and persons interested in the cure of the inebriate, urging them to bring every possible influence to bear on the Legislature by petitions to Parliament, and by special representations to every member of the Legislature, in favour of (1) the enactment of compulsory legislation of provision for the poor, and (2) the removal of present hindrances to the reception of voluntary.applicants.

div.head: "DEACON FOR WIDNES."
div.p: "DEACON FOR WIDNES."

Sir,—Recently a card bearing the heading "Deacon for Widnes" has been sent round to the various house- tolders in this district, announcing a meeting in support of the candidature of Mr. H. Wade Deacon, and I was snnewhat surprised to see how the card contradicted itself,inasmuch as the promoters had been so inconsider- ate as to give the printing of it to a firm in Liverpool, from whom no support whatever can be had in favour of his candidature. lam fully of opinion that this prin- ciple of foreign labour is totally inconsistent with the principles of Liberalism advanced by that gentleman to his constituents. Surely such an act as this should not he encouraged by his working supporters, who ought to request that all work done for or in connection with this division should be done by their fellow townsmen, whose Suffrages he is seeking. Ido not think for one moment that the candidate is responsible for this introduction of foreign work into the midst of his supporters, but at the Same time I think he should take such steps as will remedy the evil, and in future see that the work is fairly distributed in his own constituency, so that the words " Deacon for Widnes" may be translated " Widnes for Deacon" ; and I venture to add thit by so doing, his cause will be greatly enbanced. lam pleased indeed to See that a Trades Union Council is about to be formed in this district, which. I think, will go far in the direction or avoiding the introduction to this town of foreign work in all the branches of trade. Will Liverpool return the compliment and patronize this town when conducting her electoral campaigns ? Not very likely ! Since penning the above, I have been shown a card relating to another Liberal meeting, with the same printers' name at foot, as the others. This makes three examples within the past month where our trade has been given to another town.—l am, yours truly, A LOYAL TOWNSMAN.

THE TEACHINGS OF THEOSOPHY. Sir,—Having noticed in your issue of last Saturday that the Rev. J. Davies in reading a paper on Theosophy had expressed disapproval of its doctride, I shall feel obligsd if von will permit me, through the medium of your valuable columns, to state that to me it seems that the cardinal doctrine of reincarnation, at least of the lower animals, is the only theory consistent with a belief in the goodness of God and the immortality of man, for, if unprejudiced by self-conceit and unbiassed by preeenceived ideas, we reflect on what we see and know, we must acknowledge that the life of man is only life amid other life, and that our earth is only a star of earth mid other stars. Now, if there be a living creature that has more pain than pleasure, and if that creature never had life before and will never taste of life again, I fail to see how the power which brought it into being has been good to it, or how I can depend upon that power being good to me. Yet lam thankful to think that life is an inestimable blessing, and ts believe that blessing is con- tinued in another state beyond the hour of death. The inconsistency of religious teaching is the cause of so much unreality and insincerity amongst professing Christians. Let us above all things have consistency, reality, sincerity, and truthfulness. Theosophy is not at variance with the te-tchings of Christ, and it is- no more necessary for a Theosophist to believe in the Mahatmas than it is for a Christian to betieve that the world is only 10,000 years old. Science tells us that matter is indestructible, and that the chemical atoms are always the same under whatever combinations they are manifested. Is not the consciousness of a living creature of more importance than its chemical atoms, and shall this conscious life alone be blotted from the universe and those chemical atoms remain through all eternity the same ? To me it seems that a belief in the incarnation of the lower animals is the most important that mankind have ever had, for if there be no truth in it then vain are all the hones of man. Theoe,aphy teaches the gradual evolution and development of life. and a Theosophist believes— That through all nature there is wisdom, There is goodness we may bless ; Death the progress, upward, onward, To the realms of happiness. Warrington.
S. KENYON.

WHY SHOULD NOT THE EMPLOYERS' LIA- BILITY ACT BE AMENDED? Sir,—Your correspondent on the above Act, in your issue of the 20th inst., who styles himself ." a working- man" convinces me that his nom de guerre 13 WO glaringly misleading for any thinking working-man to believe that he is a working-man ; and, until he publishes his ful name and address, working-men will look upon his efforts as the stratagem of an enemy. Secondly, he cunningly impeaches our worthily much beloved work- ing-men Members of Parliament—Messrs. O'Connor, 3urt, and Broadhurst, for bringing in such a Bill, and Ireads that the Bill " is to be raised to life again in the ;oming session of Parliament." What working-man vould be so blind as to take such views of , the matters ind men involved, as your so called " Working-man " :orrespondent at Earlestown takes? Thirdly, he deplores ;he fact that Mr. Broadhurst is justly displeased with ;he Government for hitherto breaking their promises -id their present indisposition to deal as they ought to with the Bill. And were your correspondent "a work- "and had he the welfare of his class intelligently
iNintan

and deeply at heart, he would join with all the working- men M.P.'s, and the tens of thousands of the toiling mass in this country. who are also justly indignant with the present Government for the manner in which they have treated a bill so vital to the protection of the limbs and lives of poor working-men. Fourthly, your Earlestovrn correspondent either knowingly, or ignorantly, sets himself up as directly opposed to the Trades Union Con- gress held on the 10th September last, when a resolution was movedb y Mr. W. Malkin, secon.led by Mr. Fairbairn as follows :—" That this Congress expresses its strong dissatisfaction with the Government for not giving facilities for the consideration of the bill to amend the Employers' Liability Act of 1880, introduced by Messrs. Burt and Broadhurst M.P.'s., during the last session, and urges upon the Parliamentary Committee to press forward the measure again next session ; and seeing that so little attention is paid to the urgent and repeated re- presentations made to the Government on behalf of the Congress to deal with this question on the lines of the proposed bill, we urge upon the various societies and trades councils to make this a test question at the next general election." An amendment was added "with a view of modifying the right of successive appeals so un- scrupulously used by wealthy employers in defeating the ends of justice", and the resolution as amended was put, and carried unanimously. Your Earlestown correspondent would have us for- sake the wisdom and humane efforts of men like Messrs. Burt and Broadhurst ; and the united voice of the whole Congress for his assumed superior wisdom. He talks " about 170 accidents in twelve months" "in one large company's works," with as little regard for the loss of life and limb as if he were writing of as many three-inch nails accidentally bent by a railway carriage wheel run- ning over them. He utterly fails to see anything in the matter but £s. d. Loss of human life and limb are not deplored in his letter. The vital principle permeating the bill is the love of life and limb, and one speaker in the Trades Congress was not far from the mark when be stated "Capital had no conscience or any feeling, and the only way to teach it was through the pocket." The Employers' Liability Act of 1880 has been secured at an awfully high price—tens of thousands of poor working- men perishing in mines, mills, and on the sea in " cofin ships" through the heartless greed of capitalists. As the Act now stands, our poor, brave Jack Tars are only entitled to sue for compensation for injuries re- ceived while they are in a British port. Why should not the Act apply at sea to men who are on duty , there?

Your correspondent says :—" If the option of contract iq stopped, the Act will lose more that, half its value too." He means to employers who fail to make just protection for the safety of their workpeople. And working-people will then be able to find employment, whereas now they are compelled to starve, if they refuse to contract out of the Act. Such was the fate of tens of thousands of other working-men, as well as myself in the commencement of 1881, and such is still the case. Fellow-working-men, lay this motto truly to heart: Your fathers, and brothers, and sons in many cases have purchased the Employers' Liability Act by the loss of their lives and limbs. Why should you throw your own and those of your children's in the scales? If human life and limb are not to be held dearer to your heart, and the heart of the nation in general, than the cost of heartless slaughter, what is there under the whole hea- vens, social, human, moral, or divine, that can be of value to you if existence is to be flung away by con- tracting out of the Act which is given to save you? Go in for its amendm&t.—Yours truly, R. STOREY.

div.head: BRIMSTOOAN AN' TRAYCLE. (MIXED.)
div.p: BRIMSTOOAN AN' TRAYCLE. (MIXED.)
BI MAC 0' DICK 0' BOB'S. " Poncake Toosda's cOmin' on; AWII be wed to mi Uncle John."

Thad poetry isn'd hi me ; it s wod aw heeard some childer sing last week, an' aw've heeard id sung hi childer for th' last twenty odd year—nod th' same I childer o' th' time. ov coourse. Aw used to sing id I mysel' at one time, an' fro' then to neaw aw've ne'er understood why childer should tawk abeawt bein' wed to a uncle—'specially lads—a thing as th' I Prayer Book forbids. Ileaw mony dud aw ged eawtside on? Well, I aw've sin th' time when—an' thad reminds me ov a new buzz (patented i' Geo. II). A thin but growin' lad see a ;Dapper in a eytin'-heawse window one Poncake Toosda' sayin' as onybody could bey their fill o' poncakes for tourpence, "enquire within"; sooa th' lad went in, attended th' proprietor i' con- ference, an' deposited his four D—" nod necessarily for publication, but as a guarantee o' good faith." Then he geet his ears back, an' wired in. Th' fost dozen were put eawt o' sent th' best time on re- cord—ten minutes—an' when th' baker's dozen were completed th' proprietor sterted nooaticin' his cus- tomer; another hofe dozen went, an' th' lad lookt up wi' a smile, an' said: "Heigh, gaffer, let's hey a thin un this time, an' then "—"An' then! An' then wod ?" alt th' poncake manifact'rer. "An' then thicks 11118 ageean said th' lad. rh' proprietor bed bin calculatin' heaw mich th peawnd there'd be for his creditors, sooa he poo'd fourpence eawt ov his pocket an' give id to th' lad, an' said; ‘ Sitha, lad; here's thi brass back. Go hooam to thi mother an' tell her to tek tha reawnd in a penny show.' An' th' lad went, a " sadder " an' a heavier youngster. * * *

There's a gret resemblance berween poneakes an' fooak when yo' come to think things o'er i. thad leet, an' aw cud werk id eawt nicely iv aw'd nob- but Carlyle's despensia—but aw heyn'd id, thank goodness! Poncakes dorn'd wear top hats,nor gooa coourtin', but they're like fooak bon' med o' blue milk an' crate eggs i mooast cases ; some on 'em's nobbut hofe-baked,some geds"done breawn," others ged brunt, an' a lot on 'em's badly tossed. Odd tins are crisp an' good, but th' gret'st pert on 'em want moore sugar, an' they're varry heavy an' indiges- tible ; after a dose o' them soort yo' olea want a purgative to werk th' effect off. Nobbut there's this difference : poncakes nobbut trouble us wonst a .year,but these fooak as resemble th wo'st on 'em are wi' us fro' year end to year end!

Dud yo' see i'th' pappers as a Member o' Perly- rnent lied bin axin abeawt th' Balaclava heroes? He wanted to know iv it were true as th' commis- sioned officers—or mooast on 'em —were geddin' a pension; iv sooa, wod th' Government enquire into th' present position o'th' non-commissioned officers an' men as is stervin ? Thad isn'd unreasonable,an' Stanhope's answer let eawt one interestin' fact as'll encourage them as is anxious to tek a pert Ml' ferce co'd "The Charge of the Light Brigade" next time as it's to be played. This is wod Stanhope said: "The hon. member seems to be under a misap- prehension as to the conditions on which retired pay of officers and the pensions of non-commis- sioned officers and men are granted. Neither is given in consideration of any particular action or cam- paign,except in the case of wounds or broken health, but as a reward for long and faithful service. If, therefore, the officers have completed the period of service entitling them to retired pay they (like sol- diers in similar circumstances) will be in receipt of such pay. Otherwise (again like the soldiers) they will not. That's abeawt o'th' information as could be get- ten, an' aw say it's a—well never mind wod soort o'—shame. Yo' see a chap may b'e i'th Army a cer- tain length o' time beawt smellin' peawder, but he geds his pension just th' same; an' another mon may be in less time, but be face to face wi' death every bit on't, an' th' reward of his bravery is per- mission to gooa to th' werkheawse ! Heroes 'll be sca'cer nor ever when it's known as they nobbut hey abeawt a bob a week for spendin' brass, after o'th' feightin' an' nowt iv they retire too soons beawt bein' crippled for life; th' bully as con box con nick theawsands o' peawnds in a month; th Salvation Army con ax for a querter ov a million an' ged id, but th' country corn'd raise abeawt a peawnd a week apiece for this handful o' brave chaps. Aw bed thowt as th' country 'd fergetten , abeawt th' dust at Balaclava, bein' welly thirty year sin' id took place; but aw bethowt mesel' as id hed'no fergetten Marlborough—though thad may be becose th' country's memory geds nudged : occasionally, well, id owt to be nudged—an' con- tinually—i'this case, or else we's be a laughin'-stock , for other nations as wod ha' bin preawd o' sich gallant men. an ha' shown id, too.

An' this reminds me ov another veteran o'th name o' Ben Brierley as ovrt to be pensioned. There's nobody con say as he has'nd done long an' faithful service, but, th' country seems inclined to be as shabby i' this case as t'other, for id knows wad Ben's done, an' yet id says: "Well, aw'll give him fifty peawnd a year for three year, but iv he is'nd deead bi then aw—well, aw'll see." Aw'm fain to see as a tooathri chaps are tekkin' th' mat- ter up, an' aw hooap there'll be a gradely thumpin' testimonial—summat us'll tell th' country to keep fifty peawnd an' give id to somebody as id Poes°isY 'nwd need id; aw co' th' fund th' uncivil list.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 5, 1892.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 5, 1892.

Brierley seems to ha' bin varra ill for a long while, an' it's left a bit o' paralysis,, an he's nod far off his threescore an' ten, an he's bin i' harness somewheere abeawt thirty year. I' thad time he's written ten or a dozen books, an' goodness knows, heaw mony pamphlets! yigh, an' good uns, too. Tere's bits i " Layrock, o' Langleyside" as- Dhickens couldn't ha' mended, an' scoores o' theaw sands hes welly killed therael's laughing,' o'er "TA" Stuffed Monkey," an' other short readin's ; as for th'" Weyver o' Wellbrook "—well, to fratch o' thad wod be like paintin' t' lily an' gildin' refined gowd. It is a rum woild is this, when yo' come to think o' one chap as hes kept theawsands o' fooak laugh- in' o' these years bein' i' want; an' mony a one as hes spun a yarn o'er some imaginary child an' id imaginary troubles, an' med fooak cry, are wo'th a lot o' brass. Id strikes me varra foorcibly as th' best thing one con do for a livin' is to buy a big drum—but theere, aw're said enough abeawt th' Army for th' next month or two. Onyway, success to the movement, an' good health to Owd Ab.

THE CRISIS IN THE COIL TRADE. NO NEED FOR PANIC. The coal crisis has had the effect of inducing large orders, with a view of replenishing stocks. Within the past few days price have advanced for most kinds 2s. per ton. Up to the present no difficulty have been ex- perienced in obtaining coal for the steamships leaving the Mersey. The coal merchants do not anticipate that the advance will be long maintained. The Leicestershire collieries, on Thursday, intimated 1 that in future all coals will be 3s. per ton dearer. So great is the demand for household coal at Manches- ter that it is stated that the collieries in that district would require their mai output for the month to supply orders on hand. Notices have been issued at the works of the United Alkali Company at Widnes and in other parts, stating that if the collieries are stopped it will be necessary to close or partially close their works. The St. Helens collieries had not on Thursday morn- ing increased their prices, and a statement made by several newspapers on Tuesday that all the collieries at St. Helens had increased their rates was not correct. The Messrs. Pilkington have, it is believed, the largest trade in house coal in the district. On Tnursday notices wero posted in the London and North-Western Railway steam sheds at Crewe and other parts of the system stating that the company could not guarantee to find all their engine drivers and fremen regular work during the miners' strike. They enjoined on all who use coal to be as economical with it as possible. If the strike is prolonged some of the trains will be discontinued.

div.head: WARRINGTON AND THE SHIP CANAL
div.p: WARRINGTON AND THE SHIP CANAL

Yesterday a meeting of traders of Warrington and members of the Corporation was held at the Town Hall to discuss the provisions of the new Bill of the Manchester Ship Canal Company, so far as they affect Warrington, and to decide upon proposals which should be submitted to the Ship Canal Coot- pany on behalf of the borough. It was decided to ask the Company to increase the size of the proposed new lock across the river at Walton, from 125 feet by 25 feet to 150 feet by 30 feet, and to undertake to complete the lock and the connection between the canal and the river by the time the canal from Eastham to any further point was opened for treffic. It was also decided to ask the Canal Company to give Warrington the option to construct the dock itself if the Company failed to make the dock within three years. A deputation consisting of the Mayor and other representatives of the Corporation and the Chamber of Commerce, afterwards went to Manchester and waited upon the directors of the Canal Co. We be- lieve that the deputation encountered some diffi- culty in getting any further concessions from the company than they have already proposed, viz.,that they will undertake to complete the lock at Walton by the time the canal is opened for traffic, and also to complete the docks within three years after the canal hail been opened for traffic. As is known,the Corporation have petitioned against the Bill,and no doubt any further negotiations that may take place will be reserved for the Committee-rooe of the House of Lords.

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.

" Tl' TO TUN CANARY IsLANDS. Mr. R. E. Garnett, Miss Garnett, and Miss it. Garnett (who it will be 'remembered sailed a few weeks ago for the Canary Islands), have arrived safely at their destination. Letters from Maderia, announcing the news have been received by the family at Hall Nook. DEATH OF Mn. GEORGE BROADHURST. • We regret to record the death of ft.. Geo. Broad- ahurst, of Ivy House,Great Sankey,which took place ' ot his residence, on Saturday afternoon. The CitiSe yf death was bronchitis. Mr. Broadhurst was 50 tears of age, and has suffered of late from bronchi- tis, but it was not until about a fortnight ago that che illness took a serious turn. Dr. Murray was nailed in, but despite his constant attention, de- aeased gradually failed and passed peacefully away as stated. The funeral took place on Tuesday Jt St. Mary's, Great Sankey. The Rev. E. S. gackson officiated. A large number of people athered to pay the last tokens of respect to deceased. Amongst those present were Mr. Hutton Wright and wife (sister of deceased) of Leighton Hall, Neston ; Mr. Samuel and Mr. Clar- ence Wright, nephews ; Mrs. Edwin Broadhurst, Mr James Fairclough, Mr. John Robinson, Mr. John Wright, Mr. Joseph Wright, Mr. Johnson, and Mr Mainley. Messrs. Garnett and Sons were the under- takers, and Mr. E. Conner supplied the mourning equipages. There were no wreaths. Mr. Broad- hurst at the time of his death was president of the Penketh Liberal Association, and the Association's flag was flying half-mast at the club as the last token of respect for him At a meeting of the Club Committee on Monday evening a vote of condolence with the bereaved family was unani- mously passed.

div.head: CAIRO-STREET CONGREGATIONAL UNION, _ .
div.p: CAIRO-STREET CONGREGATIONAL UNION, _ .

The monthly meeting of the Congregational Union in connection with Cairo-st. Chapel, War- rington, was held on Monday evening in the school room, in Cairo-st. There was a large attendance. Mr. Monks presided, and amongst those present were the Rey. F. K. Freeston, the Rev. Joseph Freeston, the Rev. J. E. Odgers, Messrs. W. Long, F. W. Monks, Julian IVinser, Thomas Birchall, John lloughton, John Houghton, jun., and W. H. Wood- cock. Tho Chairman in his remarks said there was no doubt the monthly meetings of the Union had done much good. Referring to attendance at worship, he said there was no better training a young man or a young woman could receive than to join in the congre- gational worship on a Sunday morning and evening. Many people considered it a silly thing to be religious. He knew of no more manly or womanly conduct than to , attend public worship and to strive to lead a religious life. (Hear, hear.) He contended that their own church had done a good work for many years, and that they could look back with pride to the men who had left the congregation and had done good service in the town and neighbourhood. (Applause.) While dealing with other subjects, the Chairman also alluded to the housing Of the members of the congregation. There was no doubt that much drunkenness arose in many places owing to unhealthy dwellings and surroundings, and he though that it was part of their duty as a Christian congregat tion t-.) see that their members lived in houses that were- suitable and healthy. That was another work which, he hoped, would grow out of these meetings. (Applause.) Miss Wheeler, in the absence of Mrs. Long, presented on behalf of the ladies of the congregation, a silk gown to the Rev. F. K. Freeston, as a token of their regard for him and their appreciation of his work. The Rev. F. K. Freeston haying put on the gown, thanked Miss I Wheeler and the ladies of the congregation for their present, and the appreciation of his services. It was not the cowl that made the monk, nor the gown that made the minister, but as long as they wished their minister to wlar a gown, it should be in keeping with I their beautiful chapel.—Mr. Woodcock, as secretary of I the union, read the report of the season, and moved the re-election of the committee. The motion was seconded • by Mr. Win. Long, and carried. Mr. W. S Howard : next contributed two songs in an able manner, after which the chairman formally presented the coneregatlon with an interesting document, signed by Charles 11. and his minister, Arlington, in 1672, giving permission tc. Mr. Yates, to preach in the " Court Reuse" at Warring- ton. Other solos on the piano were contributed by Mr. Pearson. followed by refreshments and conversation. The usual votes of thanks brought the meeting to a , close.

A WARNING TO COAL DEALERS—At the Prescot Petty Sessions on Tuesday, Joseph Roby, a Whiston coal dealer was charged with selling coal from a waggon without having each bag labelled, indicating the correct weight in each sack.—lnspector Kilpatrick, proved the offence, which was committed at Prescot on the 19th ult., and defendant was ordered to pay Bs. ed., including costs.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
AT RUNCORN, &c.

".Y AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT." The thanks of the ratepayers of Runcorn, are due to Dr. McDougall for his protest against the ploughing up of the footpath leading across the fields from Greenway-road to Mill Brow. In con- sequence of this breaking of the ground,th e children I have had to travel to school through a perfect "sea of mud," and other people desirous of the short cut have had to do the same. Fortunately Victoria-road is fast approaching completion, and one of the finest roads in the town will be open for use. But neither landlord nor tenant has the right to close one foot- path until another is sqbstituted,but they frequently exercise a power they do not possess in law and the public are deprived of a convenience. In the pres- ent instance no action is necessary under the cir- cumstances, but Dr. McDougall's open condemnation will exercise a restraining influence in the future.

The subject introduced at the meeting of the School Board, on Tuesday, by Mr. Taylor is more important than at first sight may appear. The youthful mind requires something more than tbe three R's to enable it to battle successfully with the world, and its training:ought not to be confined to the rules of syntax and vulgar frac- tions. I don't intend to give an essay on morals and social culture but I think much may be done in day schools to give the young people habits that will benefit them and cling to them through life. And what habit more than thrift is essential to material success in lite ; and the earlier it is incul- cated the firmer and more deeply the habit will be fixed. The savings bank suggested by Mr. Taylor will be an admirable means of teaching the scholars how to save any stray copper they may have instead of spending them all in peg tops and bilious lollipops. The Education Department strongly advocate the establishment of these banks in schools and the postal authorities afford every facility for the easy and successful carrying on of the business. Mr. Taylor should have no difficulty in securing the end he desires.

The public of Runcorn have recently been well catered for in regard to musical entertainments, and what is a gratifying feature is that they appear to have been appreciated to the full. The third concert of the season by the Sol fa Choir was of a high class character, aucl the society is to 1:1P com- mended for the enterprise and energy that is being displayed. I hope they will close accounts with a balance on the right side, so Out they may com- mence next year work free and untrammelled and with a determination to eves excel this season's excellent record.

A general impression exists that the scholastic profession is overstocked; that teachers are swarm- ing after situations as thick as flies at the honey Jar. The experience of Runcorn School Board is all in the other direction. After weeks of advertising for an assistant master at Clreenway-road School, only two applications have been received. The first applicant was a young gentleman from Winsford, and the Clerk, Mr. Moss, in the ordinary course, waited until he had consulted his Committee be- fore arriving at a decision, and when he wrote, ap- prising the applicant of his appointment, he replied that he had accepted another situation in the interim. Anothei applicant was not forthcoming for a fortnight after this, and the Clerk, taught by experience, immediately engaged him and Mr. Daniel Green, from an unpronouncable Welsh School Board,will start his duties in Runcorn at the earliest possible moment, and Runcorn School Board are safe for the time being. But, after all, perhaps the salary of £5O a year was not a sufficiently attractive bait.

Hurrah ! Hurrah ! ! Waterloo Bridge is to be finished. Patience is rewarded at last. After twelve years of waiting, we are to have a decent throughfare across Waterloo Bridge to the station. The Commissioners have completed a very satisfac- tory agreement with Messrs. Greenall, the brewers, and an exchange of land will take place which will be of immense advantage to the town. I can imagine what a sigh of relief Mr. Pritchard will give when the Waterloo Bridge Committee dissolves, for the way the Committee have had to tread has been hard and devious.

div.head: BY AN EARLESTOWN CORRESPONDENT
div.p: BY AN EARLESTOWN CORRESPONDENT

One section, or more correctly speaking, I should say two sections of the Welshmen of Earlestown have celebrated the day of St. David, the patron saint, and it is a pity that the other section did not throw in their lot and make the celebration even more successful than it was. St. David's day is gone for this year at any rate, and on the face it appears an odd thing for the day to be honoured twice in one week. Welshmen on this occasion should show a united front, and by all means pre- vent the public outside the Welsh denominations from picking holes in their coat. I won't say any- thing more.

We in Earlestown and Ilaydock, aye and Newton too, live so to speak in the very heart of the coal trade, and yet before many days are ever, I am afraid we shall find ourselves paying a shilling per cwt. for that useful domestic commodity. Even now one dealer. I hear, is charging tenpeuce per cwt, but 1 cannot blame him. poor man—he must make hay whilst the sun shines.

Why there is all this hubbub I cannot properly understand. Perhaps I am a trifle dense ; for I cannot quite make out how ic is that immediately there is any talk of a colliers' strike, the prices should rush up so exorbitantly weeks before the strike or lockout is an accomplished fact. The coal is being obtained just as ugual, and no more is being paid for getting it, than before, and yet the suffer- ing public must bow down to an immediate increase in price.

What puzzles me more than all, however, is the seeming apathy with which the colliers View the coming strike,or whatever it is called. Going amongst the miners this week,and putting questions to them on the subject, it is surprising to find how ignorant a great many of them are as to the reason for the lockout. All many of them know about the matter is,that they are going to play a fortnight, because the delegates say they have to do. Of course, there are exceptions, and you meet with some who are very intelligent on the point, and the general im- pression appears to be that a fortnight's lockout is not the wisest course that could have been adopted

' The Conservatives are shaking themselves by the hand, and expressing satisfaction all round, at the turn in the County Council representation. They feel proud that they hold both the Parliamentary and County Council reins, and there are mysterious whispers that the Liberals were afraid to fight. I don't think they need take flattering unction to their souls, so far as regards the fighting. The Liberals were not afraid, but as Mr. Rawlins said, the honour and glory surrounding a County Coun- cillor was so infinitesimally small, that it was not worth the trouble and expense of the fight. We ratepayers also seem to be quite an insignificant quantity, when it is an uncontested election, and I think it was as little as lir. Borron could have done, to have come before us,and received our hearty good wishes. They might have stimulated him some- what in the Council Chamber. But we have not not elected him, so we are not in evidence.

div.head: DEATH OF MR. T. LOCKER.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. T. LOCKER.

It is with much regret that we announce the death of this well-known and highly respected Warringtonian. Mr. Locker had been suffering from bronchitis, and it was to a severe attack of this complaint that he succumbed, on Monday, at his residence in Church-st. Mr. Locker began busi- ness as a wire-weaver and brush manufacturer about ten years ago, and succeeded in drawing to- gether a large connection. It may be mentioned that his father before him was a well-known wire- worker, and, it is said, was the first workiaan who wove wire by steam. Mr. Locker was not a public man in the sense of having ever held public offices, but before the last municipal elections he was asked to contest Howley Ward in the Liberal interest, but this invitation he declined. The interment took 'place yesterday afternoon at the Cemetery, and amongst those present were Mr. James and Mr. T. Locker (sous), Mr. T. Kirkham (brother-in- law), Mr. T. Locker, (nephew), Mr. F. Ward (nephew), Mr. J. Wood, Messrs, W. Atherton, J. T. Hulse, Pierce Talon, J. Talon, J. Bibby, G. Wallace, J. Evans, T. Pemberton, J. E. Warren, J. R. Calvert, G. Pilling, G. Newton, and others. The Rev.. Mr, Timins, curate at the Parish Church, officiated at the graveside. The funeral arrange- ments were in the hands of Mr, J. Ronnfteld, of Butternaarket-street.

div.head: DEATH OF MR. W. SHARP OF WARRINGTON.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. W. SHARP OF WARRINGTON.

We regret to announce the death of Mr. W. Sharp, a well-known and highly esteemed Warring- tonian and a member of the firm of Messrs. R. Davies, Sharp, Kirkconnel, and Co., solicitors. The death took place on Saturday in Egypt, whither Mr. Sharp had gone for the benefit of his health. He left England for Egypt on the 22nd January last, accompanied by Dr. Henstock, of Liverpool, as friend and medical companion. After a few days at Alexandria and Cairo, the two set out for a voy- age up the Nile, meeting the Rev. Canon Under- wood,of Liverpool, and other friends, on the steamer and enjoying the sail, though Mr. Sharp complained in his letters of the great heat of the day and the coldness of the nights and early mornings. After reaching the First Cataract the party began the downward voyage with the intention of staying a week at Luxor and visiting the temples and ruins of Thebes and Karnac. In a letter, dated the 14th ult., Mr. Sharp wrote in cheerful terms, though complaining of the heat and the loss of appetite, which prevented him from doing what the others of the party did. Nothing more was heard of him until Mr. Robert Davies received a telegram on Sat- urday morning last, which had reached Warring- ton late on Friday night, from Dr. Henstock, merely stating that Mr. Sharpvvas unwell, and that they were detained at Luxor. This was followed on Saturday afternoon, by another telegram to the effect that Mr. Sharp was suffering from pneumonia and was very ill. Mr. Robert Davies replied, but at nine o'clock in the evening of the same day an- other message was received to the effect that Mr. Sharp had died that day, and was, by his own de- sire, to be buried at Luxor. In a letter, dated the 19th nit, received by Mrs. Beamont, Mr. Sharp mentions his arrival at one of the hotels at Luxor, and stating that he intended to leave Egypt for Syria and Palestine on the 10th inst. Mr. Sharp was one of the three sons of Dr. Sharp, and was never married. He was one of the trustees of the Blue Coat School, and an active member of the Infirmary Committee. He was in his 57th year. The late Mr. Sharp manifested much interest in the Blue Coat School, and every year paid the expenses of the children to Frod- sham, where they were entertained to tea. The deceased gentleman was a Churchman and a Conservative. He was a nephew of Mrs. Reamont, of Orford Hall, and a brother of the Rev. Canon Sharp, rector of Downham. On Tuesday afternoon a memorial service was held in Holy Trinity Church, the congregation of which the de- ceased was a member. He was also its lay representa- tive at the Ruri-decanal Conterences. There was a large congregation, which included the Dean of Manchester and several local and district clergymen, county and borough magistrates, members of the legal profession, a large number of other friends, as well as Mrs. Beamont and Mr. Robert Dayies. The service, which was of a most impressive character, was conducted by the Vicar of the parish, the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, and the Rector of Warrington (the Rev. F. W. Willis) The Rev. E. C. E. Carleton made a most suitable address.

It is stated that a subscription list will be opened to raise funds to place a stained glass window in Trinity Church to Mr. Sharp's memory. At the meeting of the Town Council on Tuesday even- ing, the Mayor referred to the death of Mr. Sharp. He said Mr. Sharp was a gentleman of a kind and benevo- lent disposition. He did a great deal of philanthropic work, both in money and deeds, in a quiet and unosten- tatious manner. Now he had gone they seemed to remember all the more his genial and kindly manner, and the high tone of life which they all knew had been well spent. They must all feel great grief in Mr. Sharp's death, and the town itself would mourn the loss of one of her most worthy sons, whose body now lay silent in a foreign land. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: DEATH OF AN EX-MAYOR OF WARRINGTON.
div.p: DEATH OF AN EX-MAYOR OF WARRINGTON.

We regret to have to record the death of Mr. Wm. Neild, an ex-Mayor of Warrington, which took place at Reading on Thursday night. The deceased gentleman was about 80 years of age, and was a cousin of Mr. Henry Neild, J.P., one of the Cheshire county magistrates. He was a member of t lie Society of Friends, was a native of the neighbour- hood of Weaverham, and was the owner of a small estate at that place. He was formerly a farmer at Morris Brook Farm, Latchford, and was also a partner with the late Mr. Edmund Robinson, of Bridge Mills, as a corn and flour dealer. He subse- quently became a partner in the firm of Messrs. Neild, Bleckly, and Fell, proprietors of the Dallam Forge, and when that concern was taken over by Messrs. Pearson and Knowles he went to reside at Reading, though he still retained a con- siderable interest in the business as a shareholder. He was twice married, his first wife b,dng a Mies. Wigham, a North of England lady, and his second a Miss Ellis, of Leicester. The latter died some years ago, and the deceased had since resided at Reading with his daughter. A son of his, Mr. Fredk Wm. Neild, is now residing at Chelmsford. The de- ceased was mayor in 1868-9, during the time of the election of Mr. Peter Rylands as member for War- rington. The circumstances of that period exposed Mr. Neild to a considerable amount of hostility from the Conservatives ; and, by way of counterpoise to this, the Liberals showed their appreciation, of him by presenting him with a handsome service of silver plate.
WARRINGTON MUSICAL SOCIETY'S CONCERT.

The third concert of the season given by the Warrington Musical Society, took place in the Pub- lic Hall, on Tuesday evening. The ball was crowded to excess, there being probably the largest audience that the Society have had on the occasion of one of their concerts for the last eight years. The per- formances given were Sterndale Bennett's fine cantata "The May Queen," this being rendered for the second time by the Society, who previously gave it on April 30th, 1872 ; a miscellaneous selec- tion of pieces. and Dr. H. Parry's choral ode " Blest pair of sirens." There were several unfortunate disturbances of the programme, but the Com- mittee, happily, had the opportunity to ap- prize the audience by printed circulars of the changes. Miss Eleanor Bees, contralto, and Mr. William Foxon, tenor, were prevented by illness from keeping their engagements, and their places were taken by Miss Dews and Mr..lver McKay. In the cantata the part of the "May Queen was sung by Miss Effie Thomas instead of the Princess Ahmadee, the latter lady,who,!it may be mentioned, is a Hindoo Princess, being a descenclan4 of the King,, of Delhi, singing in the second part of the programme. Mr. Barrington Foote was the baritone. It cannot be said thit the 'concert was up to the usual standard of the Society's performances. The cantata was not so harmoniously and effectively rendered as could have been de- sired. We cannot help contrasting it with the previous concert, when the" Stabat Mater," a more difficult work was performed. and when the Society appeared with some little trepidation before the public. On that occasion the performance began well and continued to go well throughout. On Tues- day night it seemed as though the concert began badly, and the artistes could never quite recover themselves thereafter. The Prin- cess, though favoured with a clamor- ous encore, with which she ccmplied, did 'not give corresponding satisfaction to the musical critics present. Miss Dews, who sang "The flight of ages;' in place of" For all eternity," was vocifenusly encored, and gave in response "The better land." Mr. Barrington Foote did much to compensate for oisappointments, and ob- tained for his fine rendering of "The night watch,"an encore, in response to which he favoured his audience with " To-merrow will be Friday." "Blest pair of sirens," was given with considerable spirit both by band and chorus. We should be sorry to have it supposed that Mr. Crossley should be held accountable for the drawbacks of the concert. He had not only worked extremely hard in rehearsing the pieces, but conducted the concert in a painstak- ing and musician-like manner.

div.head: LYMM.
div.p: LYMM.

FoornALL.—On Saturday afternoon a football' match, between Lymm Association and Manchester Grange, was played. The Lynim footballers played a good combined game, and won by five goals to their opponents' three,

, PRIMITIVE METHODIST BAND OF Hop—The Primitive Methodist Band of Hope held a service of song on Mon- day evening, entitled "Bitty and 'roe.' The service was given in the chapel, Eagle-brow. The reader was Mr. G. L. Welford. A collection was afterwards made in aid of the Band of Hope funds. ENTERTAINMENT.—On Monday evening, a concert and entertainment in connection with the Wesleyan Sunday School was given in the schoolroom. The various items were sustained by members of the select classes, assisted by friends. The programme consisted of vocal and instrumental music, &c., and concluded with an amusing diologue, entitled "Is he married ?" There was a good attendance.

div.head: STRIKE AT MESSRS. RICHMOND'S
div.p: THE STRIKE AT MESSRS. RICHMOND'S

A meeting of the Trades Council was held last night, at the Cocoa Rooms, Horeemarket-st., Mr. John Price, president, in the chair. Councillor FLOOD reported the result of the meet- ings of the deputation from the Council with the firm, which was that matters remained as before. Mr. W. 11. Bullock, secretary to the Council, read replies from Mr. Voisey and Mr. Richmond declining to be present at that meeting as they ad- hered to their former decision, and saw no advant- age to be derived from an interview with the Coun- cil.—Mr. 11. Saunders, general secretary to the stove grate workers' union, addressed the meeting, and expressed his regret that it had not to consider as to a settlement but as to carrying on the war more vigorously. A resolution was passed inviting the concurrence of the Tinsmiths' Union in sup- port of the strike.—Picketing is being continued, and the Union has sent home some 40 more of the Non-Unionist workers—about 00 in all.

div.head: NEWTON,, HAYDOCK, AND GOLBOTINE
div.p: NEWTON,, HAYDOCK, AND GOLBOTINE
BUILDING SOCIETY!:

A. specially summoned meeting of the share-- holders of the above society was held in the Town Hall, Newton, on Monday evening. Mr. J. Sankey, (chairman of Directors) presided,but there was only a moderato attendance of na,,mbarm. Thu

was called for the purpose of receiving the sanction ok the shareholders for the incorporation of tho Society under the Building Society's Act of 1874, and after some preliminary remarks, the chairman propoFed, "That the Newton, Haydock, and Golborne permanent benefit building Society, bo incorporated under the Building SocietY's Act 1874, and amended statutes, and that Mr. Joseph Jackson (a member, and one of the managers of ' the said Society) or some other person to be named by 4he meeting,. be, and is hereby authorised to make appli- cation for such incorporation."—The Managers, he said, had gone over the affairs of the Society and found they were very satisfactory. (Hear, hear.) Mr. W. Jones seconded the motion, which was supported by Mr. Lip- trott, and Mr. H. J. Langton (solicitor), who sail that the Society was solvent and able to pay 213. in the £. The resolution was put to the meeting and unanimously carried, the usual votes of thanks terminating the meet- ing.

div.head: ST. DAVID'S DAY ATTARLICSTOWN.
div.p: ST. DAVID'S DAY ATTARLICSTOWN.

On Tuesday night the Welsh Presbyterians and Independents of Earlestown celebrated the anniver- sary of their patron saint by a concert in the Viaduct Institute. These two bodies spare no effort to make the concert a success, and the quality of the artistes they secured certainly deserved a much larger audience than came together. although the attendance was very fair. Such an array of talent Is not often seen on Larlestown concert platforms, and it is not too much to say, that such a musical treat has not been enjoyed locally for a very long time. The artistes who supplied the bill of fare were Miss Alice Ainsworth (soprano), Miss Hills Burn (contralto), of the Free Trade Hall, and Newcastle Concerts, Mr. Ben Roberts (tenor), of Liverpool Cathedral, Mr. Edward Grime (St. Helens), and Mr. Leslie Harris (the Society humour- ist). The programme was a choice one, and, without exception, was rendered in a style worthy of those taking part. It included a madrigal " Brightly dawns our wedding day," from the Mikado and a quartette "Strange adventure "from the "Yeomen of the Guard." Encores were of course freely , indulged in, but in one or two instances only wore they responded to. Mr. Ben Roberts fairly thrilled the andiencs with his pure and sweet tenor, in the songs " Mona " and " Eily Mavourneen." Mr. E. Grirn&, who is well-known, was in splendid voice, and was raptur- ously applauded for his songs " Revenge" and "'Sirs, your toast " (Carmen) ; in response to a recall in the ,latter song be gave "The village blacksmith," in fine style. Miss Alice Ainsworth, with a rich, sweet soprano was greeted with tremendous applauss,. for her singing of" The Shamrock" and "Waiting," and she had to respond in each case to vociferous encores. Miss Hills Burn was not a whit behind in favour,, her rendering of " The great oak tree "from " Ruddigore," and " Nobil Signor," being remarkably fine. Miss Barfoot showed some amount of skill in her manipulation of the Welsh • national instrument, and each of her selections was redemanded. The humorous portion of the programme was undertaken by Mr. Leslie Harris, who contributed one or two excellent sketches (a la Grossrnith) in a refined and peculiarly amusing manner. Ills best effort perhaps was " The rehearsal a a pastoral cantata by a rural choral society, which was without doubt of a character too grotesque for the most cynical to withstand. Altogether the concert was thoroughly enjoyable, and the promoters are to be congratulated upon the excellency of their taste.
NATIONALIST MIILETING.

A meeting of the members of the St. Helens W. S.. Blunt Branch of the Irish National League of Great Britian was held in their rooms, Salisbury-street, on, Sunday. Mr. Boyle, district organiser, presided and be. delivered an address urging the importance and necessii-.7 of organisation amongst Irishmen. The election al officers and committee was then proceeded with. Sr. PETER'S CTICROH, NEWTON. - •

The building committee who have charge of the proposed alterations in connection with S. Paters Church, at Newton, have issued another appeal for funds, incorporated with which is a statement showing the contributions already received. The alteration, or extension, has been under considera- tion for some length of time, and it has now been decided what form the improvement shill/take. The chief alterations are in respect to the chancel, organ chamber,kc..and it is proposed to erect a, new chan— cel, remove the organ from its present position to the opposite side of the church, and thus create a south choir aisle • to remove the east wall of the church,and make the entire existing nave available for the accommodation of worshippers. Messrs. De- maize and Brierley, architects, of York, have been entrusted with the scheme, and it is estimated that the whole cost will reach something Lilco £2,50(1. Of this £2,200 has already been contributed or pro- mised, and the committeo are appealing for the rarnainder of the requireil =mut.

CHESHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL. TO THE ELECTORS OF THE RUNCORN SOUTH ELECTORAL DIVISION. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,—I have to tender you my sin- cere and heartfelt thanks for the honour you have conferred upon me in electing me unopposed as your representative in the Cheshire County Council. It will ever be my aim in the future, as in the past, to study the interests of allclasses of the community and to support all measures designed to promote their prosperity and happiness I nave the honour to remain, Ladies and Gentlemen, Yours faithfully PHILIP SPEAKMAN. The Mount. Higher Runcorn, Run corn, 29 February, 1892

COUN TY COUNCIL ELECTIONS, 1892. TO THE ELECTORS OF RUNCORN NORTH DIVISION. My Election Address having appeared in the local papers and an extended copy left at the homes of all ratepapers, and having also addressed you in public meeting, I respectfully ask for your vote to-day (Saturday), March sth, The Poll will be taken at the National Schools Church-st., and will be open from 8 o'clock in the morning until 8 o'clock In the evening. Cards containing inetructions "How to Vote," have been left with all registered electors, but should you require any further information or assistance, It will be freely given at my committee rooms. If by your favour I am elected your representative it will be my constant endeavour, in conjunction with my friend, Mr. Speakman, your member for the South Division of Runcorn, to do all I can for the prosperity of my native town. Faithfully yours, W.OOKLESTON. Halton-road, Runcorn, February 29th, 1892.

CHESHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL ELECT lON 1892. TO THE ELECTORS OF THE RUNCORN NORTH ELECTORAL DIVISION. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,— Three years ago you honoured me by electing me your Representative on the County Council, and I venture again to appeal to you for your votes and interest at the ap- proaching Election. I solicit yeur support on the same lines as I did previously —as an Independent Candidate—believing that the business of the Council is best conducted without the introduction of politics and my constant aim has been to serve the Division without respect to Party. If elected I hope to pursue in the future the same policy. I am strongly in favour of the proposed roadway across the Mersey, believing it will considerably b, neflt both Counties. Any measure having in view the adoption and maintenance of all main roads as county roads shall have my careful con- sideration and support, Technical Education shall have my best attention, but I feel that the disposal of the grants will want careful watching. Should it be your pleasure to again elect me I will do my utmost to protect your interests and advance the prosperity of this important Division. I am, Ladies and Gentlemen. Yours faithfully, C. W. lIAZLENCRST, Runcorn, February 1801.1892.

Parties whose Tenders ere accepted must enter into a written contract, and be pre- pa,-ed to enter into a bond with two sureties, if required by the Guardians.—By order of the Board, JOHN ASHTON, Clerk to the Guardians. The votes recorded on Thursday at the election in the Chertsey division, to fill the vacancy caused by the death of Mr. F. A. Hankey (C), were counted yesterday, and the result was declared as follows C. H. COMBE (C) ; 4,589 L. S BAKER (G L) . 2,751 Majority In 1888 Mr. Hankey was returned unopposed. In 1885 the Conservative majority was 1,980. YESTEItD AY'S PARLIAMENT. The first of the morning sittings of the House of Com- mons this session was held yesterday. On the motion of Mr. Bour.,Nors the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Extension to London Bill was referred to a Select Committee after considerable dis- cussion. In the evening a long discussion took place on a vote of £20,000 for the survey of the Mombasa and Nyanza Railway. The motion was ultimately carried by 211 to 113 votes,
